113d0aee3c51.headline: Stocks Had a Rough Week, but an Old Seasonal Timing Model Smells a Bounce
body: After a brutal week for the market, a well-known timing tool is flashing a more upbeat signal. According to MarketWatch, Norm Fosback's 'Seasonality Timing System' suggests stocks have an upside bias over the next two weeks.

MarketWatch describes the system as having one of the very best long-term track records among market timing models. The framing is that history, at least the calendar kind, is leaning in the market's favor after the recent sell-off.

The material available is just a headline and teaser, so details of the model's rules, its historical returns and the size of last week's losses are not part of what we can report. We won't invent them, and you shouldn't assume them either.

Some context helps. Seasonality models rest on the idea that markets tend to behave differently at certain times of the calendar, such as around month-ends, holidays or the turn of a month. Investors have studied these patterns for decades, and some of them have held up better than others.

The caveat is the usual one: a tendency is not a guarantee. A two-week upside bias means the odds may be modestly better, not that a rebound is booked like a table at a restaurant. Seasonal signals can be swamped by news, earnings, interest rate expectations or plain old panic.

For everyday investors, the sensible takeaway is probably not to trade on a calendar quirk. It is a reminder that rough weeks often feel like the start of something worse, while historical patterns sometimes say the mood may be gloomier than the odds.
113d0aee3c51.summary: MarketWatch reports that Norm Fosback's Seasonality Timing System, known for a strong long-term record, points to an upside bias for stocks over the next two weeks after a rough week.
113d0aee3c51.pixel_take: The market had a terrible week, and the calendar is basically saying, 'There, there.' Just remember that seasonal patterns are a nudge, not a promise.
113d0aee3c51.why_it_matters: Sell-offs tempt investors into rash moves, and timing models like this offer a data-driven counterweight to panic. Still, a seasonal tilt is only one input, so it should not replace diversification or a long-term plan for your money.
key_points: Norm Fosback's Seasonality Timing System is cited as having a top-tier long-term record.
It suggests an upside bias for stocks over the next two weeks, per MarketWatch.
The signal follows a brutal week for the market and is a tendency, not a guarantee.

3e2b016a40c9.headline: Democrats Eye a December Funding Fight to Force an End to the Iran War, Vietnam-Style
body: Some Democrats in Congress want to use a December 11 government funding deadline to try to force President Donald Trump to end the US-Israel war on Iran, according to Al Jazeera. The tactic carries a real risk: if the package fails, a government shutdown would begin on December 12.

The push follows this month's midterm elections, where Democrats ran on ending the conflict and won majorities in both the House and the Senate. They take control on January 3, but Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna argue that waiting is too slow. In a joint statement they urged colleagues to oppose any funding package that does not explicitly bar money for offensive operations in Iran. Senators Chris Van Hollen, Tammy Duckworth, Michael Bennet and Bernie Sanders backed similar language.

The historical model is Vietnam. In June 1973 Congress passed the Case-Church Amendment, cutting off federal funds for the war, with veto-proof support of more than two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers. Congress also overrode Nixon's veto of the War Powers Resolution that November. South Vietnam's government in Saigon fell in April 1975.

The numbers today are tougher. Republicans control Congress for another six weeks, and even in the next Congress Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats against the 67 needed to override a veto, and 257 House seats against the 290 required. Democrats have forced more than 15 war powers votes without success. A House resolution passed 220-204 in September with seven Republican votes, but Senate Republicans blocked it 51-48 last week.

The party is also split on tactics. Rosa DeLauro, set to chair the House Appropriations Committee, supports cutting off war funds but has not backed a shutdown and prefers a short-term extension over a year-long package. She questioned whether Americans would believe a shutdown ends the war. Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer have not taken a position. Republicans, while acknowledging the war's high costs, say the US must finish the job.
There is also an economic worry: critics fear a shutdown would pile onto already soaring food and petrol prices.
3e2b016a40c9.summary: Some Democrats want to attach an Iran war funding ban to the December 11 spending deadline, echoing Vietnam-era cutoffs. Party divisions, veto math and shutdown risks complicate the plan.
3e2b016a40c9.why_it_matters: A shutdown starting December 12 would disrupt federal agencies at a time when food and petrol prices are already climbing. The fight also shows how war spending and congressional leverage can shape budgets, markets and household costs.
key_points: Democrats are eyeing the December 11 funding deadline to bar money for offensive operations in Iran, risking a shutdown on December 12.
They lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a Trump veto, even in the next Congress.
Party leaders are split, with DeLauro favoring a short-term extension and Jeffries and Schumer undecided.

36ebe6cb9197.headline: Suspected Sea Drone Hits Russian Vessel at Libya's Benghazi Naval Base
body: A suspected sea drone struck a Russian vessel at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, causing an explosion and a brief fire, according to the country's eastern-based government. Reuters reported that an unspecified number of people were injured, and their nationalities were not immediately known.

The eastern administration said the ship had docked to refuel and take on supplies under a cooperation agreement between Russia and the Benghazi-based authorities. It gave no details about the vessel or its cargo. The fire has been brought under control and the site secured, it said.

No one has claimed responsibility, and there was no immediate reaction from Russia. The eastern government said it has opened a joint investigation with Moscow to establish the circumstances, the source of the attack and who was behind it.

Officials condemned the incident as a violation of Libyan sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety. They said Libya would not let its ports or waters become a place for settling scores, and stressed it is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The incident fits a wider pattern. Since the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles against Russian warships and naval facilities in the Black Sea. On Saturday, a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic near Finnish waters, which Finland's border guard attributed to Ukraine. A Russian LNG carrier sank off Libya in March, an attack Vladimir Putin blamed on Ukraine, and Ukraine said last December it struck a Russian-linked tanker in the Mediterranean.

Libya remains split between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east, and it is a focal point of Russia-West rivalry. Attribution for this latest strike is still unconfirmed.
36ebe6cb9197.summary: A suspected sea drone hit a Russian vessel at Libya's Benghazi naval base, causing an explosion, a brief fire and injuries. No one has claimed responsibility, and Russia has not yet reacted.
36ebe6cb9197.why_it_matters: Attacks on Russian-linked shipping in the Mediterranean raise risks for maritime routes and energy transport near a major oil-producing country. Any spread of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to new waters can affect shipping insurance, energy prices and regional stability.
key_points: A suspected sea drone hit a Russian vessel at Benghazi naval base, causing an explosion, fire and injuries.
No group has claimed responsibility, and Russia has not yet responded.
Eastern Libya's government opened a joint probe with Russia and said Libya is not party to the Ukraine war.

0b4f0d7826ec.headline: Intelligence chief says Putin is 'not America's friend in Ukraine,' even if Trump calls him one
body: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended President Trump's habit of calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a "friend," while insisting that the label does not describe Moscow's stance toward the United States, according to The Hill. Clayton said Putin is "not America's friend in Ukraine."

The comments, reported on November 22, 2026, draw a line between two things: the personal rapport between the two leaders and the relationship between their countries. Only the headline and teaser of the report were available, so fuller details of the remarks are not included here.

The distinction is a familiar tactic in diplomacy. Leaders often cultivate warm personal ties with rivals in the hope of opening channels for negotiation, while their governments keep competing interests firmly in place. Clayton's framing suggests the administration wants to keep both ideas alive at once: friendly words at the top, clear-eyed assessments underneath.

Still, the wording matters. Calling Putin a friend invites questions at home and abroad about how firmly Washington stands with Ukraine, and officials are frequently asked to clarify what such language means in practice. Clayton's answer appears aimed at that confusion.

For readers, the practical point is that US-Russia relations shape sanctions, energy prices and defense spending, all of which ripple into markets. Rhetoric alone moves little, but shifts in tone from senior officials are closely watched for hints about where policy on the war could go next.
0b4f0d7826ec.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended Trump calling Putin a 'friend' but said Putin is 'not America's friend in Ukraine,' separating personal rapport from the US-Russia relationship, The Hill reports.
0b4f0d7826ec.pixel_take: Friend at the personal level, not-a-friend at the national level. It's the diplomatic version of 'we're cool, but I'm not lending you my car.'
0b4f0d7826ec.why_it_matters: US-Russia relations influence sanctions, energy markets and defense budgets. Mixed signals from Washington can add uncertainty for investors watching the Ukraine war. Clarifications like this show how closely officials' wording is scrutinized.
key_points: Jay Clayton defended Trump's use of 'friend' for Putin.
He said Putin is 'not America's friend in Ukraine.'
He separated the leaders' personal relationship from the countries' relationship.

265c68ec3a4c.headline: Binding of Isaac's AI Music Scandal: Tracks Pulled, Steam Reviews Still Furious
body: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has been review-bombed on Steam for several days after players found that music in one section of the game was made with generative AI, according to The Verge. Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind the game, has since updated it to remove the offending tracks.

The discovery came from Reddit user ShweetsStuff, who looked at the songs used in a Grand Theft Auto-themed segment. They found several audio files carrying Suno metadata that pointed back to matching tracks on Suno's site.
Creator Edmund McMillen apologized on X and said he "had no idea" the GTA parody used AI-generated music. Nicalis posted on X within hours of the discovery that the generated music files were gone.

There is also a paperwork problem. Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI during development, and Nicalis does not appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere, per The Verge.

The fix has not yet repaired the damage on Steam, where the game is still rated "overwhelmingly negative." On X, users seem more willing to give McMillen the benefit of the doubt. He has been outspoken against AI in game development, and in a 2024 TikTok he called it "uninspired and bland."
The episode shows how touchy the gaming audience is about generative AI. Even a small slice of a long-running game can set off a backlash, and players are checking the files themselves.
265c68ec3a4c.summary: Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus was review-bombed after players found AI-generated Suno music in a GTA-themed segment. Nicalis removed the files and creator Edmund McMillen apologized, but Steam reviews remain overwhelmingly negative.
265c68ec3a4c.pixel_take: Nothing says 'we had no idea' like audio files with the AI tool's name stamped in the metadata. Players, it turns out, read the fine print, and the file info.
265c68ec3a4c.why_it_matters: Generative AI is spreading through game production, and audiences are policing it closely. Studios that skip disclosure rules, like Valve's requirement on Steam, risk ratings damage that can hit sales long after the content is patched out.
key_points: Players found Suno metadata in music files from a GTA-themed segment of Repentance Plus.
Nicalis removed the AI tracks within hours, and Edmund McMillen said he had no idea they were AI-made.
Steam reviews remain overwhelmingly negative, and Nicalis apparently did not disclose AI use to Valve.

493972531c14.headline: Apple's 2027 to-do list: cheaper iPads, iPhone 18e, OLED Air and smart glasses
body: Apple's packed fourth quarter of 2026 is apparently not the finish line. According to a Bloomberg report cited by Digital Trends, the company has another heavy slate of devices lined up for early 2027, following a year-end stretch that included its first foldable phone, a touchscreen Mac and new smart home gear.

The first wave is expected to land around iOS 27.4, which Bloomberg expects between February and March. It reportedly includes a new entry-level iPad, the iPhone 18e and a second-generation MacBook Neo. The standard iPhone 18 and a refreshed MacBook Air might also show up in that window.

Next comes the first half of 2027. Apple is expected to give the iPad Air an OLED screen for the first time, a display tech so far limited to the iPad Pro and the new iPad mini. A refreshed iPad Pro is also expected, along with the second-generation iPhone Air, which is rumored to swap its single rear camera for a dual setup with a primary and ultra-wide lens, like the iPhone 18.

The second half of the year reportedly brings a new Apple Watch, smart glasses, AirPods with onboard cameras and the iPhone 20. That anniversary iPhone is expected to have an all-new design, supposedly with quad-curved glass.

Don't expect everything at once. Digital Trends notes Apple will likely stagger releases, much as it split its fourth-quarter launches into separate waves for iPhone, smart home and Mac products. That also fits new CEO John Ternus's push to spread launches across more of the year, according to the report.
All of this comes from reports and rumors, not Apple announcements, so timing and specs could change.
493972531c14.summary: Bloomberg reports Apple plans a steady stream of 2027 launches, from a cheaper iPad and iPhone 18e early on to an OLED iPad Air, smart glasses and the iPhone 20 later.
493972531c14.pixel_take: Apple's calendar now looks like a fully booked dentist's office: something new every few months, and your wallet is always next in the chair.
493972531c14.why_it_matters: A staggered launch schedule gives Apple a steadier flow of revenue and headlines instead of one big holiday spike. For shoppers, budget-friendly models like the iPhone 18e and a cheaper iPad could offer lower-cost entry points, while waiting may bring OLED and new designs.
key_points: Bloomberg says a cheap iPad, iPhone 18e and MacBook Neo 2 may arrive around February to March.
An OLED iPad Air, refreshed iPad Pro and dual-camera iPhone Air are tipped for the first half of 2027.
Smart glasses, camera AirPods and the iPhone 20 are expected in the second half.

91bc026d2609.headline: Private equity's hospice shopping spree comes with a bigger Medicare bill, research finds
body: New research has found that hospice providers owned by private-equity firms cost Medicare more and keep patients enrolled longer than their counterparts, according to a MarketWatch report published November 22, 2026.

The headline finding is about two numbers moving in the same direction: higher Medicare costs and longer patient stays. The material available does not spell out the size of the gap, which providers were studied or what explains it, so those details remain open questions.

Context helps here. Private equity firms buy companies, try to improve returns and eventually sell. Hospice has drawn that kind of interest as an area of healthcare funded largely by Medicare, a government payer with predictable demand. Hospice care is meant for people near the end of life, so the length of a stay is a closely watched measure.

Longer stays and higher costs do not by themselves prove wrongdoing, and the teaser does not claim they do. But they raise the sort of questions that regulators, lawmakers and families tend to ask when profit-focused owners take over care for the terminally ill.

For taxpayers, Medicare spending is a shared bill. For investors, the research is a reminder that healthcare deals can carry political and regulatory risk alongside the promise of steady revenue. Expect the findings to be cited in debates over oversight of private equity in healthcare.
91bc026d2609.summary: New research finds hospice providers owned by private-equity firms cost Medicare more and have patients staying longer, raising questions about profit-driven ownership in end-of-life care, MarketWatch reports.
91bc026d2609.why_it_matters: Medicare is funded by taxpayers, so higher costs at private-equity-owned hospices can affect public budgets. The findings may also invite regulatory scrutiny, a risk for investors betting on healthcare roll-ups.
key_points: Private-equity-owned hospices show higher Medicare costs, per new research.
Patients also stay longer at those providers.
The findings could fuel scrutiny of private equity in healthcare.

9175c4da6624.headline: Israeli settlers attack several Palestinian villages in the West Bank, Al Jazeera reports
body: Israeli settlers attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, setting cars on fire and spray-painting racist slogans, according to Al Jazeera.
The network's correspondent Nour Odeh reported from Kafr Malik, one of the villages targeted. Al Jazeera described the incidents as part of a surge in settler attacks, which it called pogroms.

The material available gives no figures on injuries, arrests or the total number of communities hit, and it does not include any response from Israeli authorities. Those details remain unconfirmed here.

Settler violence in the West Bank has been a recurring flashpoint. The territory is under Israeli military occupation, and rights groups and international bodies have long criticized attacks on Palestinian communities and the pattern of enforcement that follows them.

Beyond the human toll, such incidents feed instability that reaches the wider region. They complicate diplomacy, add friction to relations between Israel and its partners, and weigh on the already fragile Palestinian economy, where property destruction hits households directly.
9175c4da6624.summary: Israeli settlers attacked several Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, burning cars and spray-painting racist slogans, according to Al Jazeera, which reports a surge in such attacks.
9175c4da6624.why_it_matters: Escalating settler violence deepens instability in the West Bank and can strain diplomacy and regional security. Property destruction also damages already fragile Palestinian livelihoods, and unrest in the region can influence risk sentiment and energy markets.
key_points: Settlers attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the occupied West Bank on Sunday.
Cars were set alight and racist slogans spray-painted, per Al Jazeera.
Al Jazeera reports from Kafr Malik and describes a surge in such attacks.

3cc841ff3d4c.headline: Agriculture Secretary Says U.S. Cattle Supply Is Safe, Even as Screwworm Cases Climb
body: The U.S. Agriculture Secretary has declared the nation's cattle supply safe, even as cases of screwworm in animals have risen, according to The New York Times. The reassurance came with officials saying that mitigation efforts are working well.

The officials pointed to heavy rains in the Southwest as a driver of the increase in cases. Wet weather is a notable detail here, since the report ties the uptick to conditions on the ground rather than to a failure of the response.

The material available offers few other specifics, so the number of cases, the exact locations and the details of the mitigation measures are not spelled out here. What is clear is the message from Washington: more cases, yes, but no threat to the cattle supply.

For ranchers and consumers, that distinction matters. A pest outbreak that spreads in livestock can raise costs for producers and, if it ever disrupted supply, show up at the grocery counter. Officials are betting that early reassurance and ongoing control efforts will keep that from happening.
The coming weeks will test the claim. If case numbers keep rising despite the mitigation work, the gap between a confident message and the data could become a story of its own.
3cc841ff3d4c.summary: The Agriculture Secretary says the U.S. cattle supply is safe despite rising screwworm cases. Officials blame heavy Southwest rains and say mitigation efforts are working well, according to The New York Times.
3cc841ff3d4c.pixel_take: Officials say the cattle supply is fine and the bugs are just enjoying the rain. Nothing says reassurance like blaming the weather for a worm party.
3cc841ff3d4c.why_it_matters: Livestock health feeds directly into beef supply and, eventually, grocery prices. Confidence in the cattle supply also affects ranchers' costs and how markets read agricultural risk. If the pest keeps spreading, the reassurance could be put to the test.
key_points: The Agriculture Secretary declared the U.S. cattle supply safe.
Screwworm cases in animals have risen, which officials tie to heavy rains in the Southwest.
Officials say mitigation efforts are working well.

d85a97bebee8.headline: Google's Willow Chip Wins a Four-Qubit Game Classical Computers Can't Beat
body: Google's Willow quantum processor has beaten the classical ceiling in a four-qubit coordination game, according to Decrypt. The result is being framed as a promising hardware test rather than a sign that commercial quantum computing has arrived.

Coordination games of this kind are typically used to show that quantum systems can produce correlations that no classical strategy can match. In plain terms, the setup has a hard upper limit on how well ordinary computers can play it, and Willow reportedly cleared that limit.

The details available are thin: the teaser describes a four-qubit experiment and gives no figures, timelines or methodology. So it is best read as a lab milestone, a proof that the hardware behaves in properly quantum ways, and not as a product launch.

That distinction matters. A chip beating a classical limit in a carefully designed game does not mean it can crack encryption, price derivatives or discover drugs. Those jobs need far more qubits and far better error control than a four-qubit demonstration shows.

Still, tests like this give researchers a way to check that quantum hardware is doing something classical machines cannot imitate. For an industry long accused of promising the moon and delivering a very cold refrigerator, that is a small but real step.
d85a97bebee8.summary: Google's Willow quantum processor beat the classical limit in a four-qubit coordination game, per Decrypt. It is a promising hardware test, not a sign of commercial quantum computing.
d85a97bebee8.pixel_take: Google's chip won a game classical computers can't win. Before you panic about your crypto wallet, remember: four qubits can beat a board game, not your password.
d85a97bebee8.why_it_matters: Quantum progress feeds long-term worries about the security of encryption, including the cryptography behind crypto assets. But a four-qubit game win is far from that threat, so investors should treat it as a research signal, not a market catalyst.
key_points: Google's Willow processor beat the classical limit in a four-qubit coordination game.
Decrypt describes it as a hardware test, not commercial quantum computing.
Practical uses like breaking encryption would need far larger, more reliable machines.

69216dbd1106.headline: Appeals Court Says $1.7T Biden-Era Spending Bill Was Passed Unconstitutionally via Proxy Voting
body: A federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the $1.7 trillion government funding bill Congress passed in 2022, under then-President Joe Biden, was unconstitutional, according to The Hill. The decision came from the New Orleans-based 5th Circuit.

The problem, per the ruling as described by The Hill, was how the bill got through. Lawmakers used a pandemic-era rule that allowed members of Congress to vote by proxy, rather than showing up in person. The court found that process did not square with the Constitution.

The material available so far is thin: the teaser does not spell out what the ruling means for the spending itself, whether the money already flowing under the law is at risk, or what the court's reasoning looked like in detail. Those questions will likely decide how much this matters in practice.

Context helps here. Omnibus funding bills of this size keep federal agencies running, and they tend to be passed under deadline pressure. Proxy voting was introduced during the pandemic so members could participate without traveling or gathering in crowds. Challenges to how a law was passed, rather than what it says, are unusual, which is why a ruling like this draws attention.

Expect the story to move further. Rulings from a federal appeals court can be appealed, and the next steps, whether further review or action from the government, were not detailed in the material we have. We will update as more becomes clear.
69216dbd1106.summary: The 5th Circuit ruled Friday that the $1.7 trillion 2022 funding bill was unconstitutional because Congress passed it using pandemic-era proxy voting, according to The Hill. Practical consequences remain unclear.
69216dbd1106.pixel_take: Turns out the fine print wasn't the problem with this $1.7 trillion bill. It was who showed up to vote on it. Attendance, it seems, still counts.
69216dbd1106.why_it_matters: A $1.7 trillion funding law underpins how federal agencies operate, so any legal cloud over how it passed raises questions about certainty for budgets and contractors. Markets and taxpayers will want to know whether this stays a procedural dispute or reaches actual spending.
key_points: The 5th Circuit ruled the 2022 $1.7 trillion funding bill unconstitutional.
The issue was a pandemic-era rule allowing proxy voting in Congress.
Practical effects on the spending and any appeal are not yet clear.

9cb79b635e1d.headline: Old GoPro in a drawer? Turn it into a dash cam or webcam
body: Got an old GoPro gathering dust after your last upgrade? According to Engadget, you don't have to sell it for pocket change or send it to the e-waste pile. Two easy second careers are available: dash cam and webcam.

The logic is simple. A used action camera with a tired battery isn't worth much on the resale market, but older models often still have 1080p or even 4K sensors. In both of these jobs the camera can stay plugged in, so a worn-out battery barely matters.

For the dash cam route, Engadget suggests a suction-cup mount on the windshield or dashboard, a USB connection to a port or charger, and an angle that captures a wide view of the road. Set the resolution to at least 1080p at 30 fps, and turn on loop recording, with cycles of 20, 60 or 120 minutes, so old footage is overwritten automatically. A good 64GB microSD card typically covers hours of 1080p video. After an accident, stop recording right away, or the camera may overwrite the footage you need.
Forgetful drivers have a shortcut: an experimental GoPro Labs feature can start recording whenever the camera receives USB power. It works only on models from the Hero 7 Black onward.

The webcam route is handy because many laptop webcams are low-resolution and struggle in dim light. With a Hero 8 Black or newer, you download the GoPro Webcam app, connect by USB, and the camera shows up as an option in apps like Zoom or FaceTime.

Older models take more effort. The Hero 4, 5, 6 and 7 Black have micro-HDMI ports that can feed a USB capture device such as Elgato's Cam Link 4K, which usually costs around $100. If the battery is degraded, you'll need a separate power supply. Either way, Engadget advises a mini tripod and a dedicated microphone, since the built-in mics aren't designed for video calls.
9cb79b635e1d.summary: Engadget says an old GoPro can become a dash cam or webcam with little effort. Constant USB power makes a weak battery irrelevant, though older models need extra gear for webcam use.
9cb79b635e1d.pixel_take: Your GoPro survived mountains and waves, only to be defeated by a desk drawer. Time for a second career: watching traffic and attending meetings, which some would call extreme sports.
9cb79b635e1d.why_it_matters: Reusing gear you already own saves money compared with buying a dedicated dash cam or a better webcam. It also keeps working electronics out of the e-waste stream and gets more value from past purchases.
key_points: Old GoPros can work as dash cams or webcams, and USB power makes battery wear a non-issue.
Dash cam use needs loop recording, at least 1080p at 30 fps and a decent microSD card.
Hero 8 Black and newer have a webcam app; Hero 4 to 7 Black need a capture device costing around $100.

269744fa7aca.headline: Las Vegas Could Become the Ultimate Robotaxi vs. Human Driver Test
body: TechCrunch's Mobility newsletter, published November 22, 2026, argues that Las Vegas may soon become a real-world A/B test of human-driven versus autonomous ride-hailing, after Uber added Zoox robotaxis to its app in the city.

For now, riders can't pick a robot directly. Uber customers can raise their odds of getting a Zoox vehicle and can decline a robotaxi ride, but matching is automatic when one is available. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said on the company's third-quarter earnings call that a dedicated autonomous option will come as availability and reliability improve. He added that Las Vegas will be the first U.S. city with two fully driverless partners on Uber, the other being Hyundai's Motional.
The newsletter's author notes that price could tip the balance, and wonders whether Las Vegas could become a battleground for organized labor as robotaxis compete head-on with human drivers.

On the competitive front, Tesla now has 1,507 robotaxis registered in Texas against Waymo's 1,345. The author says registrations are a weak yardstick; commercial driverless miles and miles per vehicle are better, and Waymo still leads there based on available data. That lead could shrink given Waymo's freeway setback and Tesla's Cybercab push, including a planned $3.3 billion Berlin gigafactory expansion.

Elsewhere, the Wall Street Journal reported that GM is working with an executive search firm on possible successors to CEO Mary Barra. Sources told TechCrunch the firm is Heidrick & Struggles, with names floated including Hyundai's José Muñoz, Doug Field, Larry Culp, and internal candidates Sterling Anderson and Paul Jacobson. GM declined to comment.

The roundup also covered funding rounds, including $93 million for Vincue and $45 million for Numa, Uber opening rides to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities, and Uber notifying nearly 150,000 drivers about an October data breach.
269744fa7aca.summary: Uber's addition of Zoox in Las Vegas could create a live test of robotaxis versus human drivers, while Tesla and Waymo jockey for lead and GM reportedly searches for a new CEO.
269744fa7aca.pixel_take: Vegas is about to find out whether people prefer a chatty human driver or a silent robot, with price as the house always playing the odds.
269744fa7aca.why_it_matters: Side-by-side choice in a major city will reveal how much riders value price versus a human behind the wheel, shaping the economics of robotaxis. It also affects investors weighing Tesla, Waymo and Uber, and drivers whose jobs are on the line.
key_points: Uber added Zoox to its Las Vegas app and plans a dedicated autonomous option, with Motional also a partner.
Tesla has more Texas-registered robotaxis than Waymo (1,507 vs 1,345), but Waymo reportedly leads in driverless miles.
GM is reportedly searching for a successor to CEO Mary Barra, per the Wall Street Journal and TechCrunch sources.

275fbea67a34.headline: Trump Calls Wind Power Worthless, But a Bill He Backs Could Help Build It
body: President Trump has long been one of wind energy's loudest critics, but a bill he could sign into law may end up helping wind projects move forward, according to The Hill.

Trump has called wind power "worthless" and has vowed not to approve wind energy. The teaser of The Hill's report notes, however, that he is also encouraging legislation that could have his administration advancing these projects anyway.

The full text of the original article was not available to us, so details of the bill, including what it contains and how it would affect wind permitting, are not covered here. What is clear from the report's framing is the tension: a president hostile to a technology, backing a measure that may smooth its path.

That kind of contradiction is not unusual in Washington. Big bills often bundle together many goals, and a provision one side wants can ride along with something another side prizes. A president can support a package for its main purpose while a side effect lands somewhere he has said he opposes.

For the wind industry, the story is a reminder that policy can shift even when rhetoric does not. For now, the outcome depends on whether the bill becomes law and how the administration chooses to apply it.
275fbea67a34.summary: The Hill reports that a bill President Trump could sign may have his administration advancing wind projects, even though he has called wind power "worthless" and vowed not to approve it.
275fbea67a34.pixel_take: Trump says wind power is worthless, yet a bill he likes might get turbines built. Apparently even the president's strongest opinions can be blown around by a good legislative breeze.
275fbea67a34.why_it_matters: Energy policy shapes electricity costs, investment decisions and jobs. If a bill moves wind projects forward despite the president's stance, developers and investors in renewables may gain more certainty than his rhetoric suggests.
key_points: Trump has long opposed wind energy, calling it "worthless."
A bill he could sign may let his administration move wind projects forward.
Details of the bill were not available in the source material.

4a3fc25ec61a.headline: Can't Sell? Some Homeowners Are Becoming Accidental Landlords Instead
body: Some homeowners who would once have put up a for-sale sign are renting out their houses instead, according to The New York Times. The appeal is simple: rent coming in helps cover the mortgage payment, so the house keeps paying its way.

The trade-off is that a homeowner becomes a landlord overnight, with no training. The Times reports that these new owners must learn to handle needed repairs and deal with bad tenants, jobs that can eat into the income that motivated the move.

The source material is brief, so details such as the number of people doing this, locations or rent levels are not available here. What the report does make clear is the basic bargain: steady rental income in exchange for new responsibilities.

The broader context is well known. Many owners hold mortgages they would be reluctant to replace with a new loan at different terms, and selling means giving up a home and paying transaction costs. Renting it out lets an owner keep the asset and hope it holds its value while someone else helps pay the bills.

But landlording is a business, not a passive hobby. Repairs, vacancies and difficult tenants are standard risks, and a single big fix, like a roof or a boiler, can wipe out months of rent. Anyone considering it should budget for those costs before counting on the check arriving each month.
4a3fc25ec61a.summary: Some homeowners are renting out their houses instead of selling, using rent to cover mortgage payments, the New York Times reports. The catch: repairs and difficult tenants come with the keys.
4a3fc25ec61a.pixel_take: Step one: rent out the house. Step two: discover you now work in plumbing dispatch, conflict mediation and customer complaints. The mortgage is covered, but your weekends are the new down payment.
4a3fc25ec61a.why_it_matters: Owners who rent instead of sell keep homes off the market while adding to rental supply, which can shape both housing prices and rents. For individuals, rental income can ease a mortgage, but unexpected repairs and vacancies can quickly turn a safety net into a money pit.
key_points: Homeowners are renting out houses rather than selling them.
Rent helps cover mortgage payments, per the New York Times.
New landlords must manage repairs and difficult tenants.

26541281d355.headline: SNL's 'Sister' sketch has families laughing, crying and feeling seen
body: A late-night comedy sketch from Saturday Night Live titled 'Sister' is striking a chord with families across America, according to MarketWatch, which reports that viewers are both laughing and crying over it.
The central appeal, per the outlet's teaser, is that the sketch manages to make female caregivers feel seen. One viewer reaction quoted in the headline sums it up: 'I felt so seen.'

The material available is thin: we don't have the sketch's plot, its cast, or the original article's full reporting. What can be said is that the reaction is emotional and broad, with the piece describing families across the country responding to it.

Comedy that lands this way tends to work because it names something people live with but rarely discuss. Caregiving, often unpaid and often done by women, is a daily reality for many households, and seeing it on a national stage can feel like validation.
It's a reminder that a few minutes of television can start a conversation that a stack of reports on caregiving sometimes can't.
26541281d355.summary: MarketWatch reports that SNL's 'Sister' sketch is resonating with families nationwide, drawing laughter and tears for making female caregivers feel seen.
26541281d355.pixel_take: Somewhere a caregiver just got a standing ovation from a sketch. Sadly, the sketch still can't cover the grocery run or the 3 a.m. phone calls.
26541281d355.why_it_matters: Caregiving carries real economic weight, from lost work hours to unpaid labor inside households. When pop culture spotlights it, the topic can gain attention from employers, policymakers and families planning their finances.
key_points: SNL's 'Sister' sketch is resonating with families across America, per MarketWatch.
Viewers say it made female caregivers feel seen.
Reactions mix laughter and tears, according to the report.

4064ef48a759.headline: COP31 Ends in Disaster, Even as a Super El Niño Makes Climate Change Hard to Ignore
body: The COP31 climate summit has ended in what Gizmodo describes as a disaster, with a super El Niño failing to spark the kind of action climate advocates had hoped for. The report was published on November 22, 2026.

The core of the story is a mismatch. According to Gizmodo's teaser, people can now feel climate change simply by stepping outside. But that lived experience, the outlet argues, does not automatically translate into better climate politics.

The original article's full text was not available to us, so we can't say which countries, proposals or disputes drove the summit's failure. We also have no figures on emissions pledges or funding, and we won't guess at them.

What the headline does tell us is useful context. Climate summits run on consensus among many governments with competing economic interests, and a hot summer has never been a binding treaty. Public discomfort is a powerful force, but it tends to move policy slowly, if at all.

For businesses and investors, a weak summit outcome generally means more uncertainty rather than less. Without clear global signals, companies are left to read national rules, energy prices and their own risk models, which makes long-term planning in energy, insurance and agriculture a bit harder.
4064ef48a759.summary: Gizmodo reports that the COP31 climate summit ended in disaster despite a super El Niño making climate change tangible. Feeling the heat, it argues, doesn't guarantee better climate politics.
4064ef48a759.pixel_take: Turns out you can sweat through the evidence and still not get a deal. Mother Nature sent the memo; the negotiators apparently left it in 'drafts.'
4064ef48a759.why_it_matters: A failed climate summit leaves policy signals murky, which affects energy investment, insurance costs and long-term planning for businesses. For households, weak global coordination can mean more reliance on patchy national rules while extreme weather keeps adding costs.
key_points: Gizmodo says COP31 ended in disaster.
A super El Niño did not spur climate action, per the report.
Felt climate impacts don't automatically improve climate politics.

ff69f03faa88.headline: Sheherazaad's debut LP Khudgarzi mixes Urdu folk, trip-hop and Spaghetti Western guitar, and somehow it works
body: Sheherazaad has released Khudgarzi, her debut full-length album, which is available now on Bandcamp and major streaming platforms including YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer and Qobuz, according to The Verge's review.
She first got attention in the music world a few years ago with the EP Qasr, produced by Grammy winner Arooj Aftab. The new record is described as reverb-drenched folk-noir, sung mainly in Urdu.

The sound is a deliberate collision. Traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, shares space with Arabic folk traditions and modern Western electronic music. Trip-hop touches and Spaghetti Western guitar sit alongside the tanbur and ghatam, with her voice floating over dripping percussion and woozy drones.

The album's central figure is "The Selfish Woman." Sheherazaad says she isn't a villain but a label pinned on women who defied social norms, eccentric women whose push for agency often ended badly. Tracks such as "Registaan," "Qatil" and "Zeher" explore womanhood, the legacy of colonialism and the threat of patriarchal society, per the review.

Credit goes to her production, mixing by J. Valleau and more than 30 musicians, including Ria Modak, Sarathy Korwar, Jay Chakravorty, Shunya and Qasim Naqvi. The Verge says the instrumentation never gets showy and wraps around the vocals like a shawl that is both comforting and oppressive.
ff69f03faa88.summary: Sheherazaad's debut LP Khudgarzi blends South Asian, Arabic and electronic sounds with feminist themes, sung mostly in Urdu. It is out now on Bandcamp and major streaming services, per The Verge.
ff69f03faa88.pixel_take: Trip-hop, Spaghetti Western guitar and a tanbur walk into a studio. Instead of a punchline, you get a gorgeous album. Genre purists may need to sit down.
ff69f03faa88.why_it_matters: Streaming has made it easier for genre-blending artists working in languages like Urdu to reach global listeners without a major-label push. Releases like this show where audience growth and streaming revenue can come from: niche, culturally specific music that travels well.
key_points: Khudgarzi is Sheherazaad's debut LP, mostly in Urdu, following her EP Qasr produced by Arooj Aftab.
It mixes Carnatic, Hindustani and Arabic folk with trip-hop and Western electronic elements, with 30+ musicians.
It is available now on Bandcamp, Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Deezer and Qobuz.

63e4201e02da.headline: Zelenskyy presses Washington to free paid-for Patriot missiles as Russian strikes kill five
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday urged the United States to approve delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles, after a week of Russian attacks across 20 Ukrainian regions. The latest strikes killed at least five people near Kyiv and in Zaporizhzhia, according to Al Jazeera.

In a Telegram post, Zelenskyy said Russia fired about 2,700 attack drones, nearly 1,460 guided aerial bombs and 165 missiles over the past week. Many of the missiles were ballistic, he said, including some supplied by North Korea. He said it was hard to understand the delays in delivering antiballistic systems.

His complaint is about paperwork as much as hardware. Zelenskyy said Ukraine's partners have already paid for the missiles through a NATO-coordinated programme that funds purchases of US weapons for Kyiv. Delivery is still waiting on Washington's sign-off. Ukraine is short of the US-made interceptors, which can shoot down ballistic missiles.

On the ground, a Russian strike early Sunday hit a five-storey apartment building in the village of Dymer, north of Kyiv, and part of it collapsed. Rescuers recovered three bodies and were searching for 10 missing people, including two children, Interfax reported, citing Radio Liberty. Later, a drone struck a grocery store in Vyshneve, southwest of Kyiv, killing one person and injuring three, the local governor said. A man was also killed by shelling in the city of Zaporizhzhia, according to the acting head of the regional military administration.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it hit a cargo ship northeast of Odesa, an electricity facility in Zaporizhzhia that it said supplied arms makers, an oil refinery, electrical substations and a data centre. It also claimed to have captured the village of Sosnovyi Bir in the Kharkiv region. These Russian claims could not be independently verified.
63e4201e02da.summary: Zelenskyy urged Washington to approve delivery of already-paid-for Patriot interceptors after a week of heavy Russian strikes. New attacks killed at least five people near Kyiv and in Zaporizhzhia.
63e4201e02da.why_it_matters: Delays in air-defence deliveries shape how well Ukraine can protect its cities and energy infrastructure, which affects European security and energy risk. The dispute also shows how NATO-funded arms purchases still depend on US approval, a factor for defence budgets and investors watching the sector.
key_points: Zelenskyy says Russia launched about 2,700 drones, 1,460 guided bombs and 165 missiles in a week.
Patriot missiles paid for by partners via a NATO-coordinated programme still await US approval.
Strikes near Kyiv and in Zaporizhzhia killed at least five; 10 were missing after the Dymer building collapse.

4c68479e97ae.headline: Planning for an A.I. Emergency (Or Any Calamity): A Prepper's Guide for the Rest of Us
body: The New York Times has published a piece, dated November 22, 2026, about one person's effort to prepare for the unthinkable, with an A.I. emergency as the headline example and calamities in general as the broader theme.

The material available to us is limited to the headline and a one-line teaser, so we can't tell you what specific steps the author took, what scenarios were considered, or what conclusions were reached. We won't pretend otherwise.

What the framing does tell us is that contingency planning, once the hobby of doomsday enthusiasts, is being pitched as a sensible habit for ordinary people. Putting A.I. in the same sentence as 'any calamity' signals that disruption from the technology is now treated as a plausible risk worth a checklist.

Some well-established general advice applies to almost any disruption: keep some cash on hand, hold copies of important documents, know how to reach family when networks are down, and avoid having all your finances tied to a single account or provider. None of this is specific to the Times piece, but it is the kind of groundwork emergency planners routinely recommend.

For a fuller picture, readers will want to consult the original article itself. Our take here is simply that the idea of planning ahead, boring as it sounds, tends to look brilliant only after something goes wrong.
4c68479e97ae.summary: A New York Times piece follows one person's effort to prepare for an A.I. emergency or any other calamity. Only the headline and teaser were available, so details remain unclear.
4c68479e97ae.pixel_take: Step one of any apocalypse plan: don't ask the chatbot to write it. Step two: buy batteries, the one technology that has never tried to be your coworker.
4c68479e97ae.why_it_matters: Resilience planning is cheap compared with the cost of being caught off guard, whether the shock is technological, financial or natural. As A.I. spreads into work and money, thinking about backup plans for cash, access and information becomes a practical personal-finance question.

The teaser describes one person's attempt to prepare for the unthinkable.
Full details were not available, so specifics of the plan are unknown.

bb39a2c8c643.headline: Seniors Who Shouldn't Drive Are Buying Teslas for 'Full Self-Driving' That Still Needs a Driver
body: Elderly drivers who can no longer safely handle a car are increasingly buying Teslas equipped with Full Self-Driving software, according to a Fast Company report summarized by Futurism. The catch: despite the name, the system cannot actually drive itself without a human ready to take over.

Experts quoted in the report say nobody really knows how this plays out. Johnathon Ehsani, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said how people will adopt and use these vehicles is wide open. Birsen Donmez, an engineering professor at the University of Toronto, warned that users often don't understand the systems' limits.

The appeal is easy to grasp. Giving up driving means giving up independence, and with weak public transportation in much of the US and no kids available to play chauffeur, many older people feel stuck. A car that seems to drive itself looks like a neat way out.

Tesla's messaging, critics say, nudges them along. CEO Elon Musk often says the cars can drive themselves, and the company has posted videos of owners sipping espresso while the car is in charge. Earlier this year, Tesla's North America account endorsed a video of a 71-year-old Cybertruck buyer who said his eyes were getting bad. Vehicle manuals, by contrast, say the system needs an operator ready to step in at any moment.

The branding is now officially 'Full Self-Driving (Supervised)', a parenthetical Tesla added after the California DMV sued it over misleading advertising. Unlike robotaxis from companies such as Waymo, which don't need a local human supervisor, Tesla's cars rely on the person behind the wheel.

The stakes are real. Many deaths have been linked to Tesla's self-driving tech, and last month a Tesla running FSD reportedly hit a stopped police cruiser after the driver allegedly fell asleep, sending two officers to the hospital with serious injuries. Tesla has also started recommending that drowsy drivers let FSD take over, according to the report.
bb39a2c8c643.summary: Fast Company reports that older people who can't drive safely are buying Teslas with Full Self-Driving, which still requires constant supervision. Experts warn that marketing blurs the system's limits, while crashes and legal scrutiny continue.
bb39a2c8c643.why_it_matters: Tesla's valuation leans heavily on the promise of autonomy, so gaps between marketing and reality carry legal, regulatory and reputational risk. For consumers, paying for a feature that still needs a supervising human can mean safety and liability exposure, not just disappointment.
key_points: Older people who can't safely drive are buying Teslas with FSD, per Fast Company.
Manuals require constant supervision, while marketing suggests the car drives itself.
Tesla added 'Supervised' to the name after a California DMV suit over misleading advertising.

2269595c3cbc.headline: Congress Party Youth Wing Crashes Meta's Delhi Office Over Blocked Instagram Accounts
body: Members of India's opposition Congress party protested outside Meta's offices in Delhi on Friday and appear to have entered the building, according to a video shared by CNN, as reported by The Verge. The demonstrators come from the party's youth wing.

Their demand is simple: restore the Instagram accounts of party leaders. The group also warned that more protests are on the way, so Meta's Delhi reception desk may want to stock up on visitor badges.

Two of the accounts in question were reinstated on Friday. But Manu Jain, who runs social media for the youth wing, told Reuters that thousands of accounts belonging to journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.

The protest is part of a wider fight. Congress has accused Meta of censoring speech that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party dislike, and it has put up banners around the city accusing Mark Zuckerberg of favoring the BJP.

Context matters here. In February, India tightened its rules on removing content deemed unlawful, cutting the deadline from 36 hours to just three. Modi's government has long faced criticism for restrictive free speech policies and for being accused of stifling opposition voices and pressuring the press.

For platforms, that creates a tough squeeze: move too slowly and risk running afoul of the government, move too fast and get accused of silencing critics. India is one of the biggest markets for social media, so neither option is cheap.
2269595c3cbc.summary: Congress party youth wing members protested at Meta's Delhi offices, apparently entering the building, demanding restored Instagram accounts. Two were reinstated, but the group says thousands of critics' accounts remain restricted.
2269595c3cbc.pixel_take: When your content moderation gets you a banner campaign and uninvited guests in the lobby, the three-hour takedown clock may not be the only thing ticking.
2269595c3cbc.why_it_matters: India is a huge market for Meta, so political and regulatory pressure there carries real business risk. Tight takedown deadlines and accusations of bias show how hard it is for global platforms to satisfy governments and users at once.
key_points: Congress youth wing members protested at Meta's Delhi offices and appear to have entered the building.
Two accounts were restored Friday, but the group says thousands of critics' accounts remain restricted.
India cut its deadline for removing unlawful content from 36 hours to three in February.

69d237384442.headline: Never too late to start investing, top women in finance say, and their moment may be arriving
body: MarketWatch published a piece on November 22, 2026 rounding up practical investing advice from some of the most prominent women in finance. Its central message, captured in the headline, is that it is never too late to start.

The teaser adds a broader point: there are plenty of rich and influential women in the U.S., and their time may be coming. The full text was not available to us, so we can't detail the specific tips or name the women quoted, and we won't guess.

Still, the framing fits a familiar theme in personal finance. Starting late is better than not starting, because every year invested gives money more time to grow and gives you more time to learn from your mistakes.

The teaser also hints at a shifting picture of who holds financial clout. Women in the U.S. already control significant wealth and influence, and the article suggests that role may expand. That matters to banks, advisers and fund managers, who compete for those clients.
For readers, the takeaway is simple: you do not need a perfect plan or a perfect moment. Beginning with a modest, steady habit usually beats waiting for the day everything feels certain.
69d237384442.summary: MarketWatch rounds up investing advice from leading women in finance, with the core message that it's never too late to start. The piece also suggests women's financial influence in the U.S. may grow.
69d237384442.pixel_take: The best time to start investing was years ago. The second best time is now, preferably before the next 'I'll start next month' promise to yourself.
69d237384442.why_it_matters: Starting to invest, even late, can meaningfully affect long-term savings thanks to compounding. Growing financial influence among women could also shape how the wealth management and investing industries design products and advice.

The core message: it is never too late to start investing.
The teaser suggests women's financial influence in the U.S. may be rising.

cd3f9ca39c77.headline: Fire at Indonesian confectionery factory leaves at least three dead, dozens missing
body: A fire that tore through a confectionery factory in Serang district, Banten province, western Java, on Saturday has left at least three people dead and around 36 missing, according to BBC News. The death toll is expected to rise.

The factory is about 50km west of Jakarta. Banten Governor Andra Soni said roughly 60 people were believed to be inside when the blaze began on Saturday evening. Firefighters were still fighting pockets of flame on Sunday while rescuers searched damaged sections of the building where workers were thought to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said 15 survivors had been located and four others were taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries. By Sunday evening, rescuers had recovered 24 body bags from the site. Local media reported the search was paused for the night and would resume on Monday.

Kompas TV cited a fire official as saying crews were called at 16:30 local time but found the building already engulfed. He said a large area was burning on arrival, so it was impossible to judge whether the company's fire protection system worked. The cause of the fire has not been determined.

Relatives of the missing gathered outside the factory awaiting news, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP. Search authorities say the plant is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, which describes itself on LinkedIn as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.
cd3f9ca39c77.summary: A fire at a confectionery factory in Banten, western Java, has killed at least three people, with about 36 missing. Rescuers resume searching Monday as authorities investigate the cause.
cd3f9ca39c77.why_it_matters: Industrial disasters like this put workplace safety and fire-protection enforcement under scrutiny, and can bring investigations, liability and reputational costs for companies. They can also disrupt production for a large food and beverage group's supply chain.
key_points: At least three confirmed dead, with about 36 people missing and 15 survivors located.
Around 60 people were believed to be inside the Serang factory when the fire began on Saturday.
The cause is undetermined and the search is set to resume on Monday.

72f09eb75d78.headline: Trump Says Working With Majority Leader Schumer Would Be 'Very Hard'—Schumer Must First Survive His Own Party
body: President Trump said Sunday that it would be "very hard" for him to work with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, if Schumer becomes majority leader next year, according to The Hill.

The comment lands as Schumer faces a challenge to his leadership post when Democrats gather, per the outlet's report. The teaser does not spell out who is challenging him or when any vote would take place, and the full article was not available, so those details remain unclear.

The remark is a bit of a hypothetical wrapped in a hypothetical. For Schumer to become majority leader, Democrats would first need to win control of the Senate, and he would need to keep his leadership role within his own caucus. Trump is, in effect, complaining about a job interview that has not happened for a role Schumer does not yet hold.

Still, the comment fits a familiar pattern in Washington: presidents and opposing-party leaders trade barbs long before any deal is on the table. A majority leader controls the Senate floor schedule, which gives that person real sway over which bills and nominees move forward. A president who says cooperation will be hard is signaling what the bargaining could look like.

For now, the more immediate drama is internal. Leadership challenges within a caucus tend to reveal how restless a party is, and how much its members want a different approach to confronting the White House.
72f09eb75d78.summary: President Trump said Sunday it would be "very hard" to work with Chuck Schumer if he becomes Senate majority leader, as Schumer faces a challenge to his leadership post among Democrats, The Hill reported.
72f09eb75d78.pixel_take: Trump is already griping about a boss who hasn't been hired yet. Schumer, meanwhile, has to win over his own party before he can become anyone's headache.
72f09eb75d78.why_it_matters: Who leads the Senate shapes which spending bills, nominations and policies actually move, and that affects markets and budgets. Signs of gridlock or fights over leadership can raise uncertainty around government funding and legislation.
key_points: Trump said working with Schumer as majority leader would be 'very hard'.
Schumer faces a challenge to his Democratic leadership post.
Details of the challenge were not given in the available material.

8bd939b4765a.headline: Suspected drone strike rocks Russian ship docked at Libya's Benghazi naval base
body: A Russian ship was struck in a suspected drone attack while docked at the Benghazi naval base in Libya, according to Al Jazeera. The incident reportedly caused an explosion on the vessel.

Al Jazeera also reported that another drone attack took place on a commercial vessel flying a Maltese flag off the Libyan coast. Details on the two incidents are thin so far, and the material does not say who carried out either attack, whether anyone was hurt, or how badly the ships were damaged.
The word 'suspected' is doing heavy lifting here. No party has been named in the reporting, so any attribution at this stage would be guesswork, and PixelContent will not add to the pile.

Context helps. Libya has been split for years between rival power centers, and the eastern city of Benghazi is a major hub in that map. A Russian vessel docked there shows how far Moscow's reach extends into the Mediterranean, which makes any strike on it more than a local story.

The second incident, involving a Maltese-flagged commercial ship, points to a wider risk for civilian shipping in the area. Merchant vessels in busy sea lanes tend to draw insurers' attention fast, and when attacks are reported, premiums and rerouting decisions are usually the first things to move.
More confirmed details are expected to emerge, including who was behind the attacks and what damage resulted. Until then, treat the picture as incomplete.
8bd939b4765a.summary: A Russian ship docked at Libya's Benghazi naval base was reportedly hit by a suspected drone, and a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel was also reportedly attacked off the coast, Al Jazeera says.
8bd939b4765a.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships in the Mediterranean can raise insurance costs and unsettle shipping routes that carry energy and goods. Even unconfirmed reports can make traders and insurers more cautious about the region. Geopolitical risk around Libya also matters for oil markets.
key_points: A Russian ship was reportedly hit by a suspected drone at Benghazi's naval base.
A Maltese-flagged commercial vessel was reportedly attacked off Libya's coast.
No responsible party, casualty count or damage assessment is given in the reporting.

16eaa063c1f0.headline: Retired Journalist Chuck Hubbard Ousts 11-Term Republican Virginia Foxx in North Carolina
body: Chuck Hubbard, a Democrat and retired journalist, has defeated Representative Virginia Foxx, an 11-term Republican, in a conservative North Carolina district, according to The New York Times.

The material available is thin: it does not include vote totals, the margin of victory, or details of the campaign. What is clear is the headline fact. A longtime incumbent in a district described as conservative lost to a challenger whose résumé is built on reporting rather than officeholding.

Incumbents in safe-leaning districts rarely lose, which is why this result stands out. Eleven terms means more than two decades of name recognition, committee experience and fundraising advantages. Beating that in conservative territory is the political equivalent of a rookie beating the club champion on the home course.

Without more reporting, it would be a stretch to say why it happened. Candidate quality, turnout, the national mood or local issues could all have played a part, but none of those explanations is supported by the material provided, so we will not pretend otherwise.

Expect analysts from both parties to dissect the result for clues about the national political mood and about how safe supposedly safe seats really are. Any shift in House control or margins matters for policy on taxes, spending and regulation, all of which move markets.
16eaa063c1f0.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a retired journalist, beat 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in a conservative North Carolina district, according to The New York Times, an upset for a long-serving incumbent.
16eaa063c1f0.pixel_take: A retired journalist just did what many reporters only dream of: made a powerful incumbent read the headline about herself. Deadline met, seat taken.
16eaa063c1f0.why_it_matters: Every House seat shifts the balance that shapes tax, spending and regulatory policy, which in turn affects markets and household budgets. An upset in a conservative district also signals that long-held assumptions about safe seats may be shakier than expected.
key_points: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
Foxx had served 11 terms in a conservative district.
Hubbard is a retired journalist; vote totals were not provided.

20f83d9572c0.headline: Your Ring doorbell has a social life: 11 gadget types it plays nicely with
body: Engadget has published a roundup of 11 types of smart gadgets that can be paired with a Ring doorbell, arguing that the device can do far more than announce visitors. The list covers cameras, sensors, locks, lights, thermostats, TVs, water valves, car accessories, garage openers and Amazon's Alexa gadgets.

On the security side, Ring sells more than two dozen cameras, including spotlight and floodlight models. Non-Ring cameras can join through the Ring Alarm Pro Base Station and ONVIF support, provided they are ONVIF-compatible. Ring's own panic buttons, door and window sensors, glass break sensors, sump pump monitors, smoke and carbon monoxide listeners and air-quality monitors also work, though some need the Ring Alarm Base Station hub.

Smart locks are another option. Some connect directly through the Ring app, while owning the base station widens the choice via Z-Wave. Lighting is similar: Ring's own spotlights, path lights and floodlights are supported, existing landscape lighting can join through a Ring transformer, and the outdoor smart plug can make ordinary holiday lights smart. Third-party wireless smart bulbs can't connect directly.

Inside the house, compatible smart thermostats can be controlled from the Ring dashboard. On the big screen, Amazon Fire TV devices can show the front door by voice command and pop up picture-in-picture when someone rings. Newer Samsung TVs can do it through SmartThings, though Engadget says the experience is less smooth.

The piece also highlights a smart water valve for shutting off water remotely during a leak, using Moen's app or some third-party Z-Wave valves. Ring's Car Cam and Car Tracker and Alarm bring the system into a vehicle. Compatible garage door openers can be controlled from Ring, which also enables Amazon Key in-garage delivery.

Much of this works smoothly because Amazon owns Ring, according to the article. Alexa acts as a bridge for third-party lights, plugs, thermostats, locks and TVs that don't pair directly with the doorbell.
20f83d9572c0.summary: Engadget lists 11 smart gadget types that pair with Ring doorbells, from cameras and locks to water valves, car accessories and Alexa devices, noting some need a Ring base station.
20f83d9572c0.pixel_take: Your doorbell now talks to your garage, thermostat and water valve. It's basically running a tiny, very Amazon-flavored neighborhood association, minus the angry emails about hedges.
20f83d9572c0.why_it_matters: Smart home buyers are increasingly choosing ecosystems, not single gadgets, and compatibility decides how much extra hardware they buy. Ring's ties to Amazon show how platform owners can pull more spending into their orbit. Checking compatibility first can save money on hubs and devices that don't connect.
key_points: Ring pairs with cameras, sensors, locks, lights, thermostats, TVs, water valves, car devices and garage openers.
Some accessories need the Ring Alarm Base Station, and third-party smart bulbs don't connect directly.
Amazon ownership and Alexa make integration easiest, including a bridge to non-Ring devices.

0657f5c19944.headline: Melania Trump Finds an Unlikely Diplomatic Opening in Ukraine War, Via Her Longtime Agent
body: According to The New York Times, first lady Melania Trump has developed back channels to key figures on both sides of the war in Ukraine, a role that puts her in unexpected territory for someone with little experience in international affairs.

The Times reports that she built these lines of communication through her longtime agent. The material available does not name the figures involved or describe what has been discussed, so the substance and reach of the contacts remain unclear.

What is notable is the route. Diplomacy is usually run through foreign ministries, envoys and formal summits. A channel that runs through a personal representative is closer to a private phone tree than a state department, which can be useful for quiet messages but is hard for outsiders to verify.

Informal back channels have a long history in conflict diplomacy. They can let rivals test ideas without public commitment or political cost. They also carry risks: unclear authority, mixed messages and the question of who is actually speaking for whom.

For now, the report points to a new and unconventional player in a conflict that has reshaped energy markets, defense budgets and global politics. Whether her contacts produce anything concrete is not something the available details can answer.
0657f5c19944.summary: The New York Times reports that Melania Trump, despite limited foreign-policy experience, has built back channels to key figures on both sides of the Ukraine war through her longtime agent.
0657f5c19944.why_it_matters: The war in Ukraine influences energy prices, defense spending and trade, so any possible path to talks matters to markets. Unconventional back channels could signal movement, but their unclear authority makes them a hard signal to price in.

The contacts were developed through her longtime agent.

3500af305ed0.headline: Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped prove the Riemann hypothesis, and two groups say it checks out
body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at San Francisco-based Anthropic, said on Friday that the company's Claude AI software helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. According to The Guardian, he posted the claim on his personal website and said the work took about six weeks.

On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative announced they had independently verified the result. They reviewed the solution as written in Lean, a programming language used to check mathematical proofs. The groups said they had "full confidence" the proof is correct.

The timing is awkward. Alpöge's note appeared one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and he acknowledged as much, writing that the timing was "horrible" and that he would have finished earlier if he could.

The hypothesis dates to 1859, when German mathematician Bernhard Riemann proposed it. It concerns how prime numbers are distributed along the number line. It is one of seven Millennium Prize problems chosen in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1m for each solution.

The news lands amid unease among mathematicians over AI-driven proofs. In September, OpenAI said a non-public version of its tools helped solve part of another Millennium problem, reportedly by spending $15m to run 10,000 AI systems. Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic at the time. Separately, Italian mathematician Alessandro Masullo released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis on Friday, saying he worked on it for almost 12 years and avoided AI because he did not fully trust it.
3500af305ed0.summary: An Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis in about six weeks. The Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative say they verified the proof independently.
3500af305ed0.pixel_take: Anthropic lists on Nasdaq, then casually solves a 167-year-old math puzzle the next day. Most companies just settle for a bell ringing.
3500af305ed0.why_it_matters: A verified AI-assisted proof of a Millennium problem would be a landmark for AI capability, and it could strengthen the commercial case for AI firms as investors weigh their valuations. It also sharpens debate over who gets credit, and who pays, when expensive AI systems tackle fundamental science.
key_points: Anthropic's Levent Alpöge says Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis over about six weeks.
The Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative say they verified the proof via Lean code.
The claim came a day after Anthropic's Nasdaq debut; the problem carries a $1m Clay prize.

f7ac6af79b52.headline: Measles Outbreak Hits Amish Communities, and Experts Say Trust Is the Missing Vaccine
body: A measles outbreak that has killed at least eight people in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, one in New York and one in Virginia is putting Amish and other Plain Anabaptist communities in the public health spotlight, according to The Guardian. Experts say stopping it will take trusted messengers, not just vaccine appeals.

Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner, public health researcher and clinical lecturer at Binghamton University, serves an Amish community of several hundred people in central New York. He began almost by accident, after a friend vouched for him to an Amish neighbor and word spread. A trusted messenger, he says, can be a neighbor, co-worker, customer, midwife or a driver who works for the Amish.

Sharratt argues that a sudden outbreak is the worst moment to start. Trust takes months to years, he said, and showing up only to say 'get vaccinated' will not work. He suggests informal links, such as buying vegetables at a farm stand, working alongside Amish subcontractors or visiting a bake stand every Saturday.

Beliefs and misinformation both play a part. Being unvaccinated is usually tied to plain living and the idea of Gelassenheit, or 'God's will', Sharratt said. He added that anti-vaccine activism grew alongside the Covid pandemic. Groups such as Children's Health Defense, then led by Robert F Kennedy Jr, now the US health secretary, targeted Plain Anabaptist publications.

Practical barriers matter too. Many Amish people want modern medicine when needed, but most providers take conventional insurance, while Amish communities usually rely on shared community funds. Costs can push families toward providers less tied to conventional medicine. Health departments also often lack basic data on how many people live in these communities and how many are vaccinated.

There are success stories. Sharratt pointed to the Otsego county health department, which built ties with two Amish communities two decades ago during a pertussis outbreak and still runs vaccine clinics three to four times a year. Every community differs, he stressed, but once one adopts a measure, buy-in can spread widely.
f7ac6af79b52.summary: Measles has killed at least 12 people across four states. Public health expert Tristan Sharratt says long-term relationships with Amish communities, built through trusted messengers, are essential to stopping outbreaks.
f7ac6af79b52.why_it_matters: Outbreaks in under-vaccinated rural communities show the cost of underfunded public health, from lives lost to strained health systems. Steady investment in local data and relationships is cheaper than emergency response, and it matters to any taxpayer.
key_points: Measles has killed at least eight people in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, one in New York and one in Virginia.
Sharratt says trust with Amish communities takes months to years and grows through informal, everyday contact.
Data gaps, cost barriers and anti-vaccine messaging complicate outreach, but local clinics like Otsego county's show what works.

798247febde2.headline: Husband's $80,000 boat vs. wife's $100,000 pottery studio: A couple's money spat
body: A reader's question to MarketWatch's personal-finance column has a couple at odds over spending. The husband bought a boat for $80,000, but he calls his wife's plan for a $100,000 pottery studio irresponsible. She wants to know who is right.

The only financial detail in the material is the couple's nest egg. In the teaser, the writer says they have $2.9 million in retirement accounts, including money they inherited about 10 years ago. The full column wasn't available, so we don't know their ages, income, debts, or how they paid for the boat.

The numbers still make the dispute interesting. The two purchases are within $20,000 of each other. On the face of it, one big discretionary hobby purchase has already been made, and the other is being called reckless. Whatever separates the two projects, size alone doesn't seem to be it.

Money therapists and planners often say that couples fight less about dollars than about fairness and whose priorities count. A boat and a kiln are both costly, and both can bring joy. Both can also become expensive to maintain. A studio may need equipment, materials, utilities and upkeep. A boat typically brings storage, insurance, fuel and repairs. None of those costs are described in the source, so they are general considerations rather than facts about this couple.

A sensible way to settle this kind of argument is to treat both wants by the same rules. Couples can agree on a yearly fun-money budget, set a cap on spending from retirement savings, and then judge each project on its merits. Hobby spending of $180,000 combined would be a very different matter for a household with $2.9 million than for one with $290,000, but only the household can say how much it can afford.
798247febde2.summary: A MarketWatch reader says her husband spent $80,000 on a boat but calls her $100,000 pottery studio irresponsible. The couple has $2.9 million in retirement accounts, including an inheritance.
