Like the Charmera, the SlideTag is sold in mystery boxes with retro designs, so you won't know which one you get. Collectors who dislike surprises can buy the full set of eight vintage designs for $279.92. A ninth "secret edition" with a metallic finish is available only in the individual boxes.

The design nods to the film slides once used to project photos. Instead of film, it has a 1.54-inch color E Ink screen that mixes six colored inks at 240 x 240 resolution. Don't expect LCD or OLED color accuracy, but it can hold and cycle up to 12 photos sent over Bluetooth from Kodak's Memory Link app.
The screen can also show a short to-do list, contact details, a countdown timer, or a QR code that links wherever you like. That makes it part keychain, part luggage tag, part nostalgia trinket.

As a tracker, it works with either Apple's Find My or Google's Find Hub networks. It is less capable than an Apple AirTag or Google's Pixel Tag, which use extras like ultra wideband and Channel Sounding for precise location. The SlideTag relies on basic Bluetooth, with a range of up to 30 meters in open space and a 75-decibel buzzer for close-up searching.
Power comes from a common CR2032 coin cell that is easy to replace. Battery life will depend on how often you use tracking or refresh the image.
fa0361298b06.summary: Kodak's new SlideTag, made by Reto, is a $34.99 color E Ink photo frame that also works as a Bluetooth tracker with Apple's Find My and Google's Find Hub, sold in collectible mystery boxes.
fa0361298b06.pixel_take: It's a photo frame, a tracker and a blind-box gamble in one. Finally, a way to lose your keys and your money with equal style.
fa0361298b06.why_it_matters: Nostalgia branding keeps turning cheap gadgets into collectibles, and blind-box pricing can push buyers to spend far more than the sticker price. Support for both Apple and Google tracking networks shows how those platforms are becoming a standard layer for accessories.
key_points: The SlideTag costs $34.99, or $279.92 for the set of eight designs.
A 1.54-inch color E Ink screen holds up to 12 photos, plus notes or QR codes.
It tracks via Apple Find My or Google Find Hub, using basic Bluetooth with a 30-meter range.

b6f41ac88f74.headline: Vietnam's EV Revolution Skips Cars and Hops Straight on the Scooter
body: Vietnam's streets are changing fast, according to The New York Times, as an oil shock pushes the country toward electric two-wheelers rather than electric cars.

The shift is putting pressure on global motorcycle giants that have long dominated the market, while lifting a new generation of domestic manufacturers, the report says. The material available gives only this outline, without sales figures or company names, so the scale of the change remains unclear.

The logic is easy to follow. When fuel prices jump, anyone who rides a motorbike every day feels it at the pump almost immediately. An electric bike costs less to run and is simpler to charge than a car, which makes it an obvious first step into electrification for households that never planned to own a four-wheeler anyway.

For established foreign brands, the risk is that a market they built over decades could be redefined in a few years by local rivals offering electric models. Disruption tends to arrive this way: not by beating incumbents at their own game, but by changing which game people play.

Vietnam may also offer a template for other motorbike-heavy economies. If a fuel price shock can accelerate adoption in a place where two wheels outnumber four, other developing markets may watch closely, and so will the companies that sell to them.
b6f41ac88f74.summary: An oil shock is speeding Vietnam's move to electric vehicles, but on two wheels rather than four, challenging global motorcycle giants and boosting homegrown manufacturers, according to The New York Times.
b6f41ac88f74.pixel_take: Vietnam is proving you don't need a car to have an EV revolution. Just a scooter, a fuel bill that stings, and a local brand eager to eat a giant's lunch.
b6f41ac88f74.why_it_matters: Oil price shocks can reshape consumer habits and industries quickly, especially in emerging markets. Established motorcycle makers could lose share to local challengers, and investors in autos and energy may need to watch two-wheelers as closely as cars.
key_points: An oil shock is accelerating Vietnam's shift to electric vehicles, mainly motorbikes.
Global motorcycle giants face new competition.
Domestic manufacturers are rising, per The New York Times.

4c11a1876df0.headline: Rights Group Reports 350% Surge in Attacks on West Bank Medics
body: Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said in a report released on Monday that attacks on Palestinian healthcare workers in the occupied West Bank rose by 350 percent between 2022 and 2024, according to Al Jazeera. The group says Israeli soldiers and settlers are behind the assaults, threats and intimidation.

The report is based on interviews with 25 medics. They described physical assaults, threats at gunpoint, verbal abuse and humiliating searches, and the group says this happened even when responders were clearly identifiable as medical staff. All interviewees said they live in constant fear of being stopped, attacked or kept from reaching patients.

One paramedic from the Nablus area said soldiers blocked him from reaching a wounded man he was standing close to. According to his account, the man bled until he died, and only then did the soldiers leave. An ambulance driver said every call means taking a risk, and every departure from home might be a one-way trip.

The report's author, Imran Anati, described a dangerous escalation since October 7, 2023, and called the incidents a systematic assault on Palestinian emergency medical care, for which he said Israel bears responsibility. The report also documented medics being forced to keep treating patients while facing threats themselves.

The figures fit a wider pattern. The World Health Organization recorded 233 attacks on healthcare in the occupied West Bank last year, including 165 incidents affecting medical transport. Checkpoints regularly force ambulances onto long detours, and some patients have died en route, while pregnant women have had to give birth outside hospitals. PHRI has previously warned that the West Bank medical system is collapsing.
4c11a1876df0.summary: Physicians for Human Rights Israel reports a 350% rise in attacks on Palestinian medics in the West Bank from 2022 to 2024, blaming Israeli soldiers and settlers and citing delays that endanger patients.
4c11a1876df0.why_it_matters: Attacks on emergency care deepen the humanitarian and economic strain on the West Bank, where health system breakdown raises costs and instability. Such findings can also add to international pressure and shape debates on accountability, aid and diplomatic relations.
key_points: PHRI reports a 350% rise in incidents against Palestinian healthcare workers between 2022 and 2024.
Medics describe assaults, gunpoint threats and being blocked from reaching wounded patients.
WHO recorded 233 attacks on West Bank healthcare last year, 165 affecting medical transport.

96a01e753b2c.headline: Swedish Bitcoin Treasury Firm H100 Loses 30 BTC After Trading Part of Its Own Stack
body: H100, a Stockholm-listed bitcoin treasury company, has lost about 30 BTC after moving a portion of its holdings into a derivatives trading book, according to CoinDesk. The losses, worth nearly $2 million, had built up by the end of September.

The shift came after an acquisition the company made in August. Based on the information available, H100 put a slice of its bitcoin to work in derivatives rather than simply holding it, which is the standard treasury-firm playbook turned slightly more adventurous.

The material available does not spell out which instruments the firm used, how large the trading book was, or how the company plans to respond. Those details matter, and we will not guess at them here.

The episode highlights a tension in the bitcoin treasury model. Investors in these listed companies usually buy the shares for simple exposure to BTC. Once management starts trading part of the pile, the shares also carry trading risk, and a bad run can shrink the coin count itself, not just its dollar value.

That is a different kind of loss from a price dip. If bitcoin falls, every holder suffers equally. If a treasury firm trades badly, it can end up with fewer coins than it started with, even if the market goes sideways or rises.
96a01e753b2c.summary: Stockholm-listed bitcoin treasury firm H100 lost about 30 BTC, worth nearly $2 million, after moving some holdings into a derivatives book following an August acquisition, CoinDesk reports.
96a01e753b2c.pixel_take: Holding bitcoin is hard enough for most people. H100 looked at the stack and decided to add a trading desk. Now it has 30 fewer coins and one very educational quarter.
96a01e753b2c.why_it_matters: Investors in bitcoin treasury companies often assume they are buying plain BTC exposure. Active trading with the underlying coins adds risks that can erode the stack itself. It is a reminder to read what a treasury firm does with its holdings, not just how many it owns.
key_points: H100 lost about 30 BTC, nearly $2 million, by the end of September.
The losses came from a derivatives book funded with part of its bitcoin after an August acquisition.
Details on the instruments and the company's next steps were not available.

f32fe06ee03a.headline: Van Hollen eyes Senate's top job, says Democrats' big chance comes with 'probation' strings attached
body: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is running to become the next Senate majority leader, said Sunday that Democrats have been handed a "generational opportunity" in the upper chamber, according to The Hill. In the same breath, he warned that the party is only "on probation."

The framing is classic political expectation-management: celebrate the recent Senate wins, then remind everyone that voters can take them back. Van Hollen's remarks tie the party's good fortune to what it does with it, rather than treating the wins as a permanent grant of power.

The material available is limited to the headline and a short teaser, so details of what Van Hollen said next, and what he would do as leader, are not available here. What is clear is that he is openly pitching himself for the party's top Senate post, a job that shapes the chamber's agenda, its floor schedule and how aggressively the party confronts the opposition.

Context helps. Control of the Senate decides which judicial and executive nominees get confirmed, which spending bills move, and how much leverage a party holds in budget fights. A leadership contest is therefore more than inside baseball: the person chosen sets the tone for how a new majority uses its time and political capital.

The 'probation' line also reflects a broader truth about modern American politics: majorities are narrow and fragile, and voters have repeatedly punished parties they feel overreached or underdelivered. Whoever wins the leadership race will have to convert a fleeting opening into results before the next election cycle begins.
f32fe06ee03a.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, running to be the next Senate majority leader, says Democrats have a 'generational opportunity' after recent Senate wins, but warns the party is only 'on probation' with voters.
f32fe06ee03a.pixel_take: Nothing says 'generational opportunity' like immediately reminding everyone you're on probation. Democrats are already carrying their parole officer into the leadership race.
f32fe06ee03a.why_it_matters: Who leads the Senate shapes which bills, nominees and budget deals advance, all of which can affect taxes, spending and regulation. Markets and households watch these fights because narrow majorities make policy outcomes uncertain.
key_points: Van Hollen is running to become the next Senate majority leader.
He called recent Senate wins a 'generational opportunity.'
He cautioned the party is only 'on probation' with voters.

e7f8247e4f55.headline: Goldman Sachs Sees Limited Upside for Interparfums After a 65% Share Rally
body: Goldman Sachs analysts see limited room for further gains in Interparfums after the stock's 65% rally, according to a report from Investing.com published on November 23, 2026.

The headline is the only material available, so details such as Goldman's rating, price target, and the timeframe of the rally are not known. What is clear is the core message: after a big run, the bank thinks the easy money has been made.

A 65% climb is the sort of move that raises the bar for a company. When a share price jumps that far, much of the good news is typically already reflected in it, and investors need fresh catalysts to justify paying more. Analysts often respond to such rallies by flagging that valuation has caught up with performance.

Interparfums is a name in the fragrance and beauty space, a sector investors often follow for signs of consumer demand. A cautious note from a major bank can shape sentiment, though it does not by itself change the company's underlying business.

For readers holding the stock or considering it, the takeaway is to separate a company's quality from the price paid for it. A strong business can still be an unexciting investment if the shares have already sprinted ahead. Without the full report, it is best to treat this as a signal about valuation, not a verdict on the company.
e7f8247e4f55.summary: Goldman Sachs reportedly sees limited further upside for Interparfums after its shares rallied 65%, according to Investing.com. Details of the call were not available.
e7f8247e4f55.pixel_take: After a 65% sprint, Goldman seems to be telling Interparfums investors the bottle is mostly empty on the upside. Nice scent, but the price tag already took the hint.
e7f8247e4f55.why_it_matters: A big rally can leave a stock priced for perfection, so even good companies may offer thin returns from there. Analyst caution from a major bank can influence sentiment and flows. It is a reminder to weigh valuation, not just momentum, before buying.
key_points: Goldman Sachs sees limited upside in Interparfums.
The shares have rallied 65%.
Report details such as rating and target were not available.

0839e7f144be.headline: ASUS Zenbook S14 review: a featherweight with a gorgeous screen and a 12-hour battery
body: Digital Trends has published its review of the ASUS Zenbook S14 (UX5406AA), a 14-inch ultraportable it calls one of ASUS' strongest. The reviewer used it as a main work machine for almost a month, including on a work trip to Bali, and came away impressed.

The hardware is what you would hope for: a 14-inch 2880 x 1800 OLED touchscreen with a 120Hz refresh rate, an Intel Core Ultra 9 386H chip and 32GB of memory, all in a 1.2kg body. The Ceraluminum finish gives it more personality than the typical gray slab, though the reviewer still prefers the cold, dense feel of the aluminum on the Dell XPS 14 or MacBook Air.

Battery life is the headline. With brightness at 50% to 60%, Wi-Fi on and the display left at 120Hz, the reviewer got around 12 hours of normal work and often finished the day with about 35% left. Everyday multitasking with Chrome, WordPress, Discord and Spotify ran smoothly, and in Whisper mode the fans effectively disappeared.

It is not a speed demon. Under sustained load the thin chassis limits multicore performance: the Cinebench 2024 multicore score of 709 trails the Dell XPS 14 and the Snapdragon-powered Zenbook A14. Integrated graphics managed 25 to 35 frames per second in GTA V at native resolution, so serious gamers should look for discrete graphics. The SSD was quick, with reads near 7GB/s.

The complaints are small but real. The lid can't be opened with one hand, the arrow keys are tiny, the glossy screen picks up reflections, and the finish shows fingerprints. The reviewer also wants a haptic touchpad on a laptop at this price, since the mechanical click feels dated, especially near the top edge.
0839e7f144be.summary: Digital Trends calls the ASUS Zenbook S14 a light, elegant ultraportable with a superb 120Hz OLED screen and roughly 12 hours of battery life, held back by modest sustained performance and a few annoyances.
0839e7f144be.pixel_take: Twelve hours of battery and a featherweight body, yet it still can't open with one hand. Even great laptops have to leave something to complain about.
0839e7f144be.why_it_matters: Ultraportables are increasingly judged on real-world endurance rather than benchmark bragging rights, and this review shows where thin Intel designs stand against Snapdragon rivals. For buyers, it is a reminder to match a laptop to how they actually work, not to peak specs.
key_points: Around 12 hours of battery at 120Hz in normal work, per Digital Trends
3K OLED touchscreen, Core Ultra 9 386H, 32GB RAM, 1.2kg
Sustained multicore and gaming performance are limited by the thin chassis

4cd515da3b85.headline: Built to Whisper, E.V.s Now Want to Growl Like Gas Engines
body: Electric cars were sold on silence, but some automakers now want their EVs to make a lot more noise. According to The New York Times, designers working on upcoming electric supercars from Lexus and Ferrari are looking at ways to give those cars a roar, as a way to help them stand out.

The irony is hard to miss. For years, a hushed cabin and a quiet street were part of the pitch for going electric. Now the performance end of the market seems to be asking whether a car that goes fast without any drama can still feel like a supercar.

The source material is limited to a headline and teaser, so details on how these sounds will be produced are not available here. The teaser does make clear that there are two different goals. High-end performance cars want a signature sound to build personality and presence, while quieter city-bound models are trying to be good neighbors.

That split reflects a basic design question. Sound is part of how drivers judge speed and character, and part of how pedestrians notice a vehicle. Engine noise has long been a selling point for performance brands, so losing it creates a gap that engineers and marketers now want to fill deliberately.

For buyers, this means the sound of a car is becoming a software-driven design choice rather than a byproduct of combustion. Brands that sell on emotion may treat it as a feature, while makers of everyday urban EVs may keep things subtle. Either way, the debate shows how automakers are working out what a car should feel like when the old rules no longer apply.
4cd515da3b85.summary: The New York Times reports that designers of upcoming electric supercars from Lexus and Ferrari want their cars to roar, while quieter city EVs aim to be good neighbors.
4cd515da3b85.pixel_take: EVs spent a decade bragging about silence, and now the supercars want a megaphone. Next up: a Prius that clears its throat before a meeting.
4cd515da3b85.why_it_matters: As electric cars replace combustion engines, sound becomes a designed feature that can help luxury brands protect their emotional appeal. That matters for how automakers differentiate products and justify premium prices in a market where performance is increasingly similar.
key_points: Lexus and Ferrari have electric supercars on the way, according to The New York Times.
Designers hope a roaring sound will help these cars stand out.
Quieter city-bound EVs are instead trying to be good neighbors.

756073f765a5.headline: Australia's treasurer warns jobless rate will top 5% as growth sags and inflation lingers
body: Australian treasurer Jim Chalmers has told parliament that "things will get a bit harder before they get easier", revealing that next month's mid-year budget update will show unemployment rising above 5% and slower growth for the next two years, according to The Guardian.

Speaking in a ministerial statement during question time, Chalmers called the coming numbers "concerning". Inflation, now at 4.7%, is forecast to ease only to the "mid-3s" by the middle of next year, roughly one percentage point higher than the May budget assumed, with high fuel costs to blame. Growth is expected to stay below 2% in both 2027 and 2028.

The warning follows last week's news that unemployment rose to 4.9% in October. That has sharpened fears that five Reserve Bank rate hikes are biting harder than expected, with their full effect likely to show up through 2027.

Shane Oliver, AMP's chief economist, expects growth to slow from 2.3% to below 1%. He said Australia "could flirt with recession next year" and put the odds of a more severe downturn at a high and rising 40%. He also expects official figures on Wednesday to show inflation approaching 5%.

Chalmers is trying to thread a needle. A majority of Australians blame public spending for this year's inflation surge, so he promised the update will contain budget-sized "net savings" that more than offset new spending, though it is not a mini-budget full of new initiatives. One example is the $25 prescription price cap, extended to the end of the decade at a cost of $242m. He insisted there would be no slashing of services.

There is a catch. A weaker economy and big unavoidable commitments mean larger deficits in the later years of the forward estimates. Chalmers argued it would be irresponsible to fully offset the automatic hit to revenue and payments. Oliver called the task a difficult balancing act: cut too little and the political heat stays on, cut too much and recession risk grows.
756073f765a5.summary: Treasurer Jim Chalmers says Australia's mid-year update will show unemployment above 5%, growth under 2% and stubborn inflation, as economists warn of a rising recession risk and the government promises net savings.
756073f765a5.pixel_take: Australia's treasurer is promising to cut spending enough to calm inflation but not enough to cause a recession. It's the economic version of defusing a bomb while being told to hurry up.
756073f765a5.why_it_matters: Rising unemployment, sticky inflation and repeated rate hikes squeeze households and could shape mortgage costs and job security in Australia. Government spending cuts that are too steep could deepen a slowdown, while too little restraint keeps price pressure alive.
key_points: Unemployment is forecast to exceed 5% after hitting 4.9% in October, with growth under 2% in 2027 and 2028.
Inflation, now 4.7%, is expected to fall only to the mid-3s by mid-2027, about 1 point above May forecasts.
AMP's Shane Oliver puts recession odds at 40%, as the government promises net savings but bigger later deficits.

42a8c67d6cb6.headline: Cardano holders are balking at a $4 million bill for the Foundation's flagship 2027 event
body: Cardano's governance process is giving the Cardano Foundation's 2027 conference budget a chilly reception. According to CoinDesk, voting stake opposing the roughly $4 million request outweighs stake backing it by about five to one.
The proposal covers the cost of running the network's flagship event. Holders who vote with their stake appear unconvinced, at least so far, that a big conference deserves that much treasury money.

The picture looks different for another request. CoinDesk reports that a developer tools proposal filed on Nov. 16 faces almost no opposition, suggesting holders are not against spending in general, only against some kinds of spending.

That contrast is the real story. On-chain governance lets token holders act like shareholders at a very public budget meeting, and they can vote down costs that look like marketing while waving through work that builds the product. Developer tooling tends to be easier to defend than a conference, because its results can be measured in apps and builders rather than in lanyards and keynote slots.

The source material is thin on details, such as final vote totals, the voting deadline or the exact breakdown of the conference budget, so it is too early to say whether the request will fail outright or be reworked. Still, a lopsided early tally is usually a hint to go back and sharpen the pitch.
For anyone holding ADA, this is a live test of whether community treasury governance has teeth when a major institution asks for money.
42a8c67d6cb6.summary: Cardano holders are voting heavily against the Foundation's roughly $4 million 2027 conference budget, while a developer tools request filed Nov. 16 meets almost no resistance, according to CoinDesk.
42a8c67d6cb6.pixel_take: Turns out Cardano voters will happily fund the tools that build things, but a $4 million party with a name badge is a tougher sell. Governance: where the crowd checks the receipts.
42a8c67d6cb6.why_it_matters: Treasury votes show whether decentralized governance can actually restrain spending by influential organizations. For holders, how a network's funds are allocated affects its long-term development and, indirectly, the value of the token.
key_points: Voting stake opposing the roughly $4 million 2027 conference budget is about five times the stake supporting it.
A developer tools request filed Nov. 16 faces almost no opposition.
Holders appear to favor building-focused spending over event costs.

72880452e0e7.headline: Sen. John Kennedy Says He Might Run in 2028 If He Gets 'Really Fed Up'
body: Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, said Sunday that he could seek the presidency in 2028 if he becomes "really fed up," according to The Hill. It is less a campaign launch than a conditional threat, the political equivalent of saying you might cook dinner if the takeout is bad.

Kennedy made clear that his current plan is to run for reelection to the Senate. He said he has been saving up his "nickels and dimes," and put the total at about $30 million. The teaser cuts off as he says he will add a few more, so we don't have the rest of his remarks.

The full text of the interview was not available, so details on the setting, what exactly might push him over the edge, and any other plans remain unknown. What is clear is that he is keeping the door open without walking through it.

Context helps here. A war chest of roughly $30 million is a substantial sum for a senator's reelection effort, and it gives a lawmaker flexibility. Senators float presidential ambitions fairly often, and a hint of a White House run raises a politician's profile, draws media attention and can help with fundraising, whether or not a campaign follows.
For now, 2028 is still a long way off, and Kennedy's own stated plan points to the Senate. Whether his frustration level rises enough to change that is the open question.
72880452e0e7.summary: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said he plans to seek Senate reelection but could run for president in 2028 if he gets "really fed up." He said he has saved about $30 million.
72880452e0e7.pixel_take: A presidential run powered by frustration and nickels and dimes. Somewhere, a campaign consultant just heard a cash register and a sigh at the same time.
72880452e0e7.why_it_matters: Early talk about 2028 shapes donor behavior, party maneuvering and media attention long before any ballots are cast. A senator with a $30 million war chest is a player in fundraising and policy debates, which can matter to markets watching Washington.
key_points: Kennedy said Sunday he could run for president in 2028 if he gets "really fed up."
His current plan is to run for Senate reelection.
He said he has saved about $30 million.

a3559e9bacb2.headline: JPMorgan Sees Asian Stocks Bouncing Back After the Great Positioning Unwind
body: JPMorgan is flagging the potential for a sharp rebound in Asian equities after investors unwound their positions in the region, according to a headline from Investing.com published on November 23, 2026.

The source material available is limited to that headline, so details such as the size of the unwind, the specific markets involved, price targets or the bank's timeline are not known. Anything beyond the core call would be guesswork, and we would rather not guess with your money.

Still, the logic behind the idea is a familiar one in markets. When investors rush to cut exposure, selling can push prices down further than economic fundamentals alone justify. Once that wave of selling fades, there are fewer sellers left, and even modest buying can lift prices quickly.

That is the basic case for a rebound after a positioning unwind: the crowd has already left the room, so the room has space for new arrivals. Whether Asian stocks actually follow that script depends on factors the headline does not describe, including earnings, currencies, interest rates and global risk appetite.

For now, this is a view from one major bank, not a guarantee. Bank forecasts can be useful signposts, but they are opinions about an uncertain future, and markets have a long record of ignoring them when it suits them.
a3559e9bacb2.summary: JPMorgan sees potential for a sharp rebound in Asian equities after a positioning unwind, according to Investing.com. Details of the call were not available.
a3559e9bacb2.pixel_take: After everyone sprints for the exits, JPMorgan points out the party might get good again. Classic markets: the crowd leaves, then the snacks look great.
a3559e9bacb2.why_it_matters: Asian equities are a large part of many global and emerging-market funds, so a rebound call can influence how investors position. Positioning-driven swings can move prices fast in both directions, which matters for anyone holding regional ETFs or pensions with Asian exposure.
key_points: JPMorgan sees a potential sharp rebound in Asian equities
The call follows a positioning unwind by investors
Details of the forecast were not available in the source material

60e1740ca2cc.headline: Kodak's SlideTag turns a keychain into a tiny photo frame that also helps you find your keys
body: Kodak has announced the SlideTag, a keychain-sized digital photo frame that doubles as a Bluetooth tracker, according to Digital Trends. It costs $34.99 and is sold through the company's official store. It is made by Reto under a Kodak license.

The design nods to the 1935 Kodachrome slide mount. The screen is a 1.54-inch, 6-color E Ink display at 240 x 240 pixels. Using Kodak's Memory Link app over Bluetooth, owners can load up to 12 photos from a phone. It can also show contact details, to-do lists, countdown timers and QR codes.

On the tracking side, the SlideTag works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub. It uses Bluetooth 5.4 with a range of up to 30 meters in open areas, and a 75dB buzzer rings when you get close. It has a user-replaceable CR2032 battery and an IP54 rating. The device measures 39.3 x 46 x 7.58mm and weighs 16.6 grams.

There is a catch for precision hunters: it lacks ultra-wideband connectivity, which trackers such as the Apple AirTag 2 and Google Pixel Tag offer. That makes it less exact when you are searching for something nearby.

Then there is the gamble. The SlideTag is sold in blind boxes with eight standard designs and one secret metallic edition, which has a 1-in-64 chance of turning up in a single box. A full set costs $279.92. Each box also includes a battery, a collector's poster, a slide frame and a mini film strip.

Buyers can order two single units and one set at a time, and orders cannot be canceled or changed once placed. A one-year warranty covers manufacturing issues. The launch follows the popularity of Kodak's tiny Charmera camera.
60e1740ca2cc.summary: Kodak's $34.99 SlideTag is a color E Ink keychain that shows up to 12 photos and works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub. It's sold in blind boxes and lacks UWB.
60e1740ca2cc.pixel_take: Kodak has built a keychain that shows your memories, finds your keys and sells you the thrill of a gacha draw. Nostalgia now comes with odds: 1 in 64.
60e1740ca2cc.why_it_matters: Licensed heritage brands are increasingly selling nostalgia as collectible hardware, and blind-box pricing can push shoppers to spend more, like the $279.92 full set. It also shows how Apple and Google's tracking networks let small makers add finding features cheaply.
key_points: $34.99 SlideTag has a 1.54-inch, 6-color E Ink screen and holds up to 12 photos
Works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub but has no UWB for precise nearby tracking
Sold in blind boxes: eight standard designs, one secret edition at 1-in-64 odds, full set $279.92

1e3834cb7a60.headline: Pip Assessments Face a 'Fundamental Overhaul' as Timms Review Lands Tuesday
body: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms says the assessment process for the personal independence payment (Pip) needs a "fundamental overhaul". His year-long review of disability benefits is due to be published in full on Tuesday, according to BBC News. He wrote in the Times that the current setup is "no longer fit for purpose".

Timms said Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, but that disability and ill health have shifted in the 13 years since. He pointed to substantial growth in claims linked to mental health and neurodiverse conditions, plus changes in wider society and the workplace.

The headline proposal is a "fast track" route for people with the most severe conditions and those receiving end-of-life care. It would be less burdensome and would free up assessment capacity for other cases. Timms argued that someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not face regular reassessments that feel adversarial and unnecessary.

The review follows a political scramble. It was commissioned after former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government U-turned on a plan to cut the welfare bill by £5bn a year. More than 130 MPs, 120 of them Labour, backed an amendment against the 2025 cuts, citing the number of people who could be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation.

A week earlier, a separate review led by former Labour Health Secretary Alan Milburn recommended moving 18-to-24-year-olds off Pip and the health element of universal credit onto a new system. The government accepted that, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the same philosophy could apply across the age range. How the two reviews fit together is still unclear.

The money at stake is large. Pip is expected to cost more than £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020, and had 4m claimants as of 30 April 2026, according to the Department for Work and Pensions. Charity Scope warned that ministers must not weaken the benefit, saying many disabled people fear being unable to afford essentials.
1e3834cb7a60.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms will recommend a fundamental overhaul of Pip assessments, including a fast track for severe conditions. His review lands Tuesday, as Pip costs head toward £41bn by 2030.
1e3834cb7a60.why_it_matters: Pip is a huge and fast-growing item in the welfare budget, so any redesign affects both Treasury spending and household finances for millions of claimants. Changes to assessments could shift public spending forecasts and political fights over welfare.
key_points: Timms says Pip assessments need a fundamental overhaul and are no longer fit for purpose.
A fast track would cover severe conditions and end-of-life care, with fewer reassessments.
Pip is forecast to cost over £41bn by 2030, with 4m claimants as of April 2026.

ad3cbc391bb1.headline: China's Military Eyes A.I., but Fears It Could Expose Its Nuclear Arsenal
body: Chinese military researchers are working on ways to use artificial intelligence, but they also worry the technology could leave China's nuclear forces more exposed to attack, according to The New York Times.

The headline of the report frames the concern as a fear of a nuclear checkmate: the idea that A.I. could help an adversary find, track or target the weapons a country counts on to deter a strike. The material available gives only that outline, with no further detail on specific studies, researchers or systems.

The worry rests on how nuclear deterrence works. A country that believes it can absorb a first strike and still hit back is less tempted to strike first, and less likely to be attacked. If new tools make a nation's retaliatory forces easier to locate or destroy, that logic gets shakier, and so does the stability built on top of it.

That makes the story a useful reminder that the A.I. arms race is not only about who builds the smartest system. It is also about what those systems might reveal about an opponent's defenses. Beijing is reportedly pursuing military uses for A.I. while fretting about the very vulnerabilities the technology could open up.

Because the original article text was not available, PixelContent cannot detail what the researchers concluded or how their concerns might shape Chinese policy. What the teaser makes clear is that anxiety about A.I. is not confined to any one capital, and that nuclear stability is now part of the conversation.

e104b0170769.headline: Planet X2: Scientists Say Another World May Lurk Beyond Neptune
body: Astronomers may be inching closer to answering one of the solar system's longest-running whodunits: is there another planet hiding beyond Neptune? According to Interesting Engineering, scientists have unveiled new clues about a hypothesized object being called Planet X2.

The details are thin. The original article text was not available to us, and the teaser only says researchers may be one step closer to solving a big mystery of our cosmic neighborhood. We therefore can't tell you how big the proposed planet is, where it might be, or what evidence the team is pointing to.

What we can say is that the idea of an undiscovered world in the distant outer solar system has been a recurring theme in astronomy. The far reaches beyond Neptune are dark, cold and enormously large, which makes any faint object there very hard to spot. Researchers usually look for indirect hints, such as odd patterns in how distant objects move, and then try to confirm them with telescopes.

Until a telescope actually catches such a planet in the act, claims like this stay in the category of promising clues rather than settled fact. Expect plenty of follow-up observations, debate and healthy skepticism before anyone updates the textbooks.
We'll update this story if fuller details of the research become available.
e104b0170769.summary: Scientists have reportedly unveiled new clues about a possible hidden planet beyond Neptune, dubbed Planet X2, according to Interesting Engineering. Details of the evidence are not yet available.
e104b0170769.pixel_take: The solar system may have a hidden roommate beyond Neptune. Astronomers have found clues, but so far the planet hasn't answered the door.
e104b0170769.why_it_matters: Discoveries in deep space drive demand for better telescopes, sensors and data-processing tools, which feeds research funding and the tech sector. For readers, it's mostly a reminder that even our own cosmic backyard isn't fully mapped.

Astronomers are described as possibly one step closer to solving the mystery.

8d5cc95a3523.headline: MSCI weighs Plan B for Indonesia after talks with Prabowo, per Investing.com
body: MSCI, the index provider whose benchmarks steer huge amounts of global investor money, is considering alternatives to downgrading Indonesia, according to a headline from Investing.com published on November 23, 2026. The reconsideration follows talks involving Indonesian President Prabowo.

The material available is just that headline, so details are thin. We do not know what the alternatives are, who took part in the talks, or what timeline MSCI is working to. Treat anything beyond the basic outline as unconfirmed for now.

Still, the broad stakes are well understood. MSCI decides how countries are classified and weighted in its indexes, and a downgrade in market status can prompt funds that track those indexes to sell. Even the threat of one can rattle local stocks and the currency, because passive money tends to follow the rulebook rather than the mood.

The fact that MSCI is exploring other options suggests the downgrade is not yet a done deal, and that dialogue with Indonesian authorities may be shaping the outcome. Index providers usually prefer a consultation and a fix over a dramatic reclassification, though any decision rests with MSCI.
For now, investors in Indonesian assets are left watching for the next announcement, which will show whether the country dodges the penalty box or merely gets a softer version of it.
8d5cc95a3523.summary: MSCI is reportedly considering alternatives to downgrading Indonesia after talks with President Prabowo, according to Investing.com. Details on the options remain unavailable.

2a01fd54249f.headline: Vietnam's E-Bike Boom Turns Ordinary Homeowners Into Charging Entrepreneurs
body: Vietnam is swapping gas-powered motorbikes for electric two-wheelers at a rapid pace, and homeowners are building an informal charging economy around the shift, according to The New York Times. The trend has been accelerated by the war in Iran, the outlet reports.

The details available are limited, but the headline and teaser sketch a clear picture: the people powering the surge are not big utilities or energy giants. They are entrepreneurial homeowners who have found a way to turn a plug and a bit of space into a business serving riders who need a charge.

The geopolitical link is the key context. When conflict in the Middle East rattles oil supplies, fuel prices tend to become less predictable, and drivers in fuel-importing countries feel it at the pump. In a country where motorbikes are a central part of daily transport, a switch to electric models is a practical way to sidestep that exposure.

Informal charging networks also fill a gap that formal infrastructure often struggles to cover. Building public charging stations takes time, money and planning. Households that already have electricity and a doorstep can respond far faster, much like corner shops appear wherever customers gather.

The shift is worth watching beyond Vietnam. If high fuel costs push riders toward electric vehicles, and small-scale entrepreneurs build the support system, it offers a model for other emerging markets where two-wheelers dominate the roads. Questions about safety, regulation and power demand will likely follow, but the NYT's reporting suggests the market is moving ahead of the rulebook.
2a01fd54249f.summary: The war in Iran is driving a fast switch from motorbikes to e-bikes in Vietnam, and entrepreneurial homeowners are building an informal charging economy to serve riders, according to The New York Times.
2a01fd54249f.pixel_take: Geopolitics shakes the oil market, and somewhere in Vietnam a homeowner shrugs, points at a power outlet and opens for business. Gas stations, meet the living room.
2a01fd54249f.why_it_matters: Oil shocks from conflicts can push consumers toward electric transport faster than policy alone. Grassroots charging businesses show how new energy markets can grow without waiting for big infrastructure. For investors, it signals shifting demand in a major two-wheeler market.
key_points: Vietnam is rapidly shifting from motorbikes to electric two-wheelers.
The war in Iran is cited as the catalyst, per The New York Times.
Homeowners are creating an informal charging economy.

2648c1cdf9ec.headline: Displaced Lebanese families return to ruins in Nabatieh as Israeli attacks continue despite ceasefire
body: Displaced families in Nabatieh, in southern Lebanon, have been returning to their communities to find ruins and widespread destruction, according to Al Jazeera. The report was published on November 23, 2026.

Israeli attacks in the region are continuing even though a ceasefire has been in place since April, Al Jazeera reported. That leaves returning residents in a difficult position: they are going back to damaged areas while strikes have not fully stopped.
The report also links the situation to a broader political question. It says the ongoing attacks raise doubts about Lebanon's sovereignty, 83 years after the country gained its independence.

The source material offers limited detail on casualties, the scale of damage in figures, or the specific incidents behind the continuing attacks, so those points remain unclear. Nothing in the report describes what reconstruction plans, if any, are under way.

Stories like this follow a familiar pattern in post-conflict zones. A ceasefire on paper does not automatically restore safety, housing or services, and families often return before basic infrastructure has been rebuilt. That tends to leave local economies stalled and households carrying the cost of repairs themselves.
2648c1cdf9ec.summary: Displaced families are returning to ruins in Nabatieh, southern Lebanon, while Israeli attacks continue despite an April ceasefire, Al Jazeera reports, raising questions about Lebanese sovereignty.
2648c1cdf9ec.why_it_matters: Continued strikes under a nominal ceasefire keep reconstruction and investment risk high in southern Lebanon. Israeli attacks continue despite a ceasefire in place since April, per Al Jazeera.
The attacks raise questions about Lebanon's sovereignty 83 years after independence.

e24fc9fb1bdf.headline: Nvidia Brings Jensen Huang Back as CEO, Days After Board Said No Return
body: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, only days after its board had ruled out his return, according to Decrypt. Shares reportedly jumped 26% in premarket trading on the news, which was reported on November 23, 2026.

The board's stated reason for the turnaround is notable. It said input from senior U.S. officials left it confident that Huang's return poses no national security risk. The material available does not say what the concern was, how Huang left the role, or which officials were consulted.

That leaves a lot of open questions, and we will not guess at them. What the reporting does establish is the sequence: a board decision against his return, a reversal within days, and a market reaction large enough to make the reversal look like the main event.

A 26% premarket move is a big number for any company. It suggests investors treated Huang's presence as central to Nvidia's value, not just a line on an org chart. When a founder-style leader is seen as inseparable from a company's strategy, leadership changes can move the stock as much as earnings do.

The explicit reference to national security also shows how closely chipmakers are now tied to government views. Companies that make critical technology often find that personnel decisions, not just products and exports, can draw official attention. For now, the board says it is satisfied, and the market clearly agrees.
e24fc9fb1bdf.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO days after ruling out his return, citing input from senior U.S. officials on national security. Shares reportedly surged 26% premarket, according to Decrypt.
e24fc9fb1bdf.pixel_take: Nvidia's board went from 'he's not coming back' to 'welcome back' faster than most of us can finish a streaming trial. The stock, at least, approved of the plot twist.
e24fc9fb1bdf.why_it_matters: A 26% premarket jump shows how much investors tie Nvidia's value to its leader. For anyone holding Nvidia directly, through index funds or in AI-related bets, leadership stability can swing portfolios sharply. It also shows how national security views can reach into corporate governance at major chipmakers.

The board cited input from senior U.S. officials that his return poses no national security risk.
Shares reportedly rose 26% premarket, according to Decrypt.

c32e65acfc49.headline: CrowdStrike Agrees to Buy Zscaler in $43.9 Billion All-Stock Cybersecurity Mega-Merger
body: CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9 billion, the two companies announced on Monday, according to TechCrunch. It is a blockbuster pairing in the cybersecurity world, and it is aimed squarely at the AI era.

Zscaler, based in San Jose, California, sells cloud security products to about 8,000 enterprise customers. Its specialty is zero-trust technology, which makes employees prove who they are every single time they access an internal system or resource. The idea is that a hacker holding stolen credentials still cannot wander freely around a company's network.

CrowdStrike comes at the problem from a different angle. It protects the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a company's network. The companies say that merging its endpoint protection software with Zscaler's zero-trust platform will give customers "superior protection" against data breaches.

The pitch also leans heavily on artificial intelligence. The companies said the combination will create the "largest single addressable market" in cybersecurity and help customers adopt AI safely, a theme that is hard to avoid in any tech announcement these days.

The deal still needs regulatory approval and is expected to close around this time next year. Because it is paid in stock rather than cash, the transaction depends on the value of CrowdStrike's shares, and regulators will decide whether combining two big security vendors raises competition concerns.
c32e65acfc49.summary: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock, combining device protection with zero-trust security. The companies say it will help customers adopt AI safely. Regulatory approval is needed, with closing expected in about a year.
c32e65acfc49.pixel_take: Zero trust meets endpoint protection: the only merger where both sides will presumably ask each other for ID at the door, every single time.
c32e65acfc49.why_it_matters: A deal of this size signals that companies are consolidating security vendors as AI changes how businesses handle data and access. Investors in cybersecurity stocks should watch regulators and CrowdStrike's share price, since the all-stock structure ties the deal's value to the market. Enterprise customers could see fewer, bigger security platforms to choose from.
key_points: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth $43.9 billion.
Zscaler's zero-trust platform serves about 8,000 enterprise customers and will join CrowdStrike's endpoint protection.
The deal needs regulatory approval and is expected to close around this time next year.

0770198fefa0.headline: Deer Wedges Itself Between House and Deck in Wisconsin, Police Called
body: A deer in Wisconsin found out the hard way that not every gap is a shortcut. According to UPI, police responded to a home where the animal had wandered into the narrow space between the house and a wooden deck and ended up wedged there.

For homeowners, the episode is a small lesson in how wildlife interacts with the spaces we build. Gaps beside decks, porches and foundations can look like nothing to us but can be an inviting, and inescapable, passage for a curious animal. If an animal is trapped, the usual advice is to call local authorities or wildlife officials rather than attempt a rescue yourself, since a frightened deer can be unpredictable.

512453057e1c.headline: Nvidia soars 30% as Jensen Huang returns as CEO, dragging tech stocks along for the ride
body: Nvidia shares opened up 30% in New York on Monday after the chipmaker reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive with immediate effect, according to BBC News. The move added roughly $1 trillion to the company's market value.

The reversal is a whiplash one. Less than two weeks earlier, Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and Nvidia's shares had fallen significantly in the interim. The board voted unanimously to bring him back after what the company called a series of discussions and meetings with him.

The rally spread well beyond one company. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 6.5% in early trading. Microsoft and Amazon each gained nearly 4%, while Apple rose less than 2%. Other chipmakers did even better: Micron Technology jumped 19%, Intel climbed 14% and AMD gained nearly 7%. Much of the buying began in pre-market trading, before Huang's return was announced, following heavy tech losses on Friday.

Friday was ugly for Nvidia in particular. Its shares fell nearly 14% after Reuters reported, in a claim the BBC has not confirmed, that the US Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating the company's accounting practices. Monday's bounce comes on top of that cloud, not after it has cleared.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage XTB, called Huang the 'godfather' of AI with a 'talismanic influence over the sector'. She noted that although he holds no special voting shares, the directors evidently could not picture the company without him.
Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, since its chips are central to the industry. That is why one executive's job status can move not just one stock but a whole corner of the market.
512453057e1c.summary: Nvidia shares jumped 30% after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned. The Nasdaq rose 6.5% in early trading as chip and tech stocks rallied.
512453057e1c.pixel_take: Two weeks out, one unanimous board vote back in, and a trillion dollars reappears. Most of us can't get a refund on a toaster that fast.
512453057e1c.why_it_matters: Nvidia is so central to the AI trade that a single leadership decision swung the Nasdaq by 6.5% and moved rivals and big tech alike. For anyone with index funds or retirement accounts, it shows how concentrated market performance has become in a few AI-linked names. The reported SEC probe remains an unresolved risk.
key_points: Nvidia opened up 30%, adding about $1 trillion in market value, after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.
The Nasdaq rose 6.5% early; Micron gained 19%, Intel 14% and AMD nearly 7%.
Shares had fallen nearly 14% Friday on unconfirmed reports of an SEC accounting investigation.

143cfc55d1d6.headline: Your Closed Support Tickets Might Be AI Training Gold, Says a Data-Licensing Startup
body: SourceX, a Los Angeles-based company, is pitching businesses on an idea: the old support tickets, finished projects and documented workflows sitting in their software could be licensed as training and evaluation data for AI, according to a sponsored-style piece published by Digital Trends on November 23, 2026.

The company says it licenses approved operational business data directly from firms. Potential sources include support conversations, documented workflows and internal company knowledge. The argument is that a full record, from the question to the attempted fixes to the final outcome, shows how a business actually solves problems, which is more useful than a pile of disconnected messages.

On the process, SourceX says companies approve the scope and then sign with it, and the firm handles agreements, data preparation, delivery and payment. It describes de-identifying data before use or onward sharing. The material itself cautions that this does not replace a review of privacy, confidentiality and contractual restrictions. An initial fit check requires no record uploads, only a description of the records.

Money is where the fine print matters. SourceX advertises substantial potential payments for large enterprise datasets, but says the upper figure is neither typical nor guaranteed, and that actual deals depend on qualification, dataset fit and signed terms. It also runs a referral program, including an optional bonus of 20% of directly invited partners' eligible paid rewards, one level only. Rewards require qualifying transactions, acceptance, payments and approval, and signups alone earn nothing.

The suggested first step is practical: work out which records your company controls and who is authorized to discuss them. Describing the system, the time period and the kinds of completed work is enough to start. The text frames the key question as whether the archive fits, not how big an export can be.
Readers should note the piece is promotional in nature and carries a disclaimer that it is not legal or financial advice.
143cfc55d1d6.summary: SourceX says companies could license approved records like support tickets and workflows to train AI. It advertises large potential payouts, but stresses they are not typical or guaranteed and depend on qualification and signed terms.
143cfc55d1d6.pixel_take: Your closed tickets finally get a second career. Just make sure legal reads the contract before your 2019 customer rants become a machine's bedtime stories.
143cfc55d1d6.why_it_matters: AI developers need high-quality, real-world data, and that is turning internal company archives into a possible new revenue stream. But privacy, confidentiality and contract risks are real, and advertised payouts are best-case figures, so companies should do legal due diligence before sharing anything.
key_points: SourceX licenses approved business records such as support conversations and workflows for AI training and evaluation.
Advertised payouts are upper bounds, not typical or guaranteed, and depend on qualification and signed terms.
De-identification is described, but companies still must review privacy, confidentiality and contract limits.

1cb78417896f.headline: White House says Trump was 'totally involved' in bringing Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
body: The White House is taking a victory lap over Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, first reported by Semafor, that President Donald Trump was "totally involved" and that the board made a great decision, according to The Verge.

Trump repeated the point on CNBC, saying the US has to "protect our geniuses." He said he "believed very strongly" that Huang should return, and claimed that without his involvement Nvidia would have had a very sad stretch ahead.

On the investigation, Trump said it showed Huang had shown bad judgment in what he called somewhat unrelated incidents, but had done nothing wrong. On Truth Social, he wrote that the government has no reason to believe Huang's return poses a national security risk, and that the Attorney General confirmed it has no evidence of unlawful conduct by him.

Nvidia's own announcement points the same way. The company said its board received input from senior levels of the US government that made it confident reinstating Huang would not create a national security risk. That followed reports about Huang's involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

The timeline adds to the picture. Less than 12 hours before the decision, Trump posted that bringing Huang back would be the best thing for Nvidia and the country, and urged the board to rehire him. Semafor now reports he also called into the board meeting around that time to argue the same case.
It is an unusual spectacle: the head of a government publicly claiming credit for a private company's personnel call, while the company itself cites government input as a reason for the decision.
1cb78417896f.summary: The White House says Trump was 'totally involved' in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, and Nvidia says it received input from senior US government levels on national security concerns.
1cb78417896f.pixel_take: Nvidia's board meeting apparently had a surprise guest on the line. Corporate governance, now featuring a very persuasive speakerphone.
1cb78417896f.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the most valuable and strategically important chips companies, so who runs it matters to investors and to US-China tech policy. Open government involvement in a boardroom decision raises questions about governance and political risk for companies in sensitive sectors.
key_points: White House and Trump say he was 'totally involved' in Huang's reinstatement.
Nvidia says its board got input from senior US government levels on national security.
Semafor reports Trump called into the board meeting to urge the rehire.

5566b456d1b7.headline: Leaked death certificates reveal Russia's hidden war toll: over 460,000 dead, little ground gained
body: A Guardian analysis of leaked Russian death certificates has produced the most detailed picture yet of Moscow's losses in Ukraine, identifying more than 460,000 war-linked deaths between the February 2022 invasion and September 2026. The data comes from more than 11 million certificates obtained by the Belarusian-linked Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.

The records, compiled by Russia's statistics agency Rosstat, show a war growing steadily deadlier. Almost 20,000 deaths were logged in the first year and 50,000 in 2023. The toll then topped 134,000 in 2024 and rose a further 52% in 2025 to close to 200,000, or about 548 men a day, against an average of roughly 277 since the start. Russia's defence ministry last updated its official figure in September 2022, at 5,937.

The scale dwarfs recent comparisons, according to the Guardian. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers died over nine years in Afghanistan. In one week from 5 May 2025, Russia lost more men than the US did in eight years in Iraq. In 2025, war became the leading cause of death for Russian men under 65, cited in 29% of certificates with a recorded cause.

The payoff on the map has been thin. Since the start of 2023 Russia has gained about 8,000 sq km, under 1.5% of Ukraine, according to DeepState. Nearly 116,000 deaths with a known location were in Pokrovsk district. After Avdiivka fell, about 88,700 Russian soldiers were recorded as dying there while troops advanced 39km, more than 2,200 per kilometre.

Analysts say the losses are biting. Janis Kluge of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs said falling recruitment combined with heavy losses apparently forced Russia to slow attacks in 2026. The average age at death has risen from 34 to nearly 40, as the Kremlin leans on cash bonuses rather than a second unpopular mobilisation. The true toll is probably higher, since missing soldiers are often registered months or years later.
5566b456d1b7.summary: Leaked death certificates analysed by the Guardian show more than 460,000 war-linked Russian deaths since 2022, peaking in 2025, while territorial gains stayed small and the losses deepen Russia's demographic and manpower problems.
5566b456d1b7.why_it_matters: Heavy losses and a shrinking pool of recruits strain Russia's labour market, budget and long-term demographics, all of which shape the war's duration and the outlook for sanctions, energy markets and European security spending.
key_points: Guardian analysis found over 460,000 war-linked Russian deaths from February 2022 to September 2026.
2025 was deadliest, with close to 200,000 deaths, about 548 a day.
Russia gained about 8,000 sq km since 2023, under 1.5% of Ukraine, per DeepState.

93b5534af2ec.headline: Bitcoin bounces back above $63,000 after a liquidation-fueled tumble
body: Bitcoin climbed back above the $63,000 mark after a selloff driven by liquidations, according to Investing.com, which reported the rebound on November 23, 2026.

The source material is thin on details, so the exact size and timing of the drop are not available here. What the headline does make clear is the mechanism: the slide was tied to liquidations rather than a single named piece of news.

Liquidations happen when traders who borrowed money to bet on price moves are forced to close their positions because their collateral no longer covers the loan. When prices fall quickly, those forced sales can push prices lower still, which triggers more liquidations. It is a bit like a domino rally where the dominoes are leveraged bets.

The flip side is that such selloffs can reverse quickly once the forced selling runs out, since the drop reflects mechanics more than a change in long-term views. A rebound above $63,000 suggests buyers stepped in after the shakeout, though one bounce does not tell us whether the move will last.
For anyone watching crypto, the episode is a reminder that leverage amplifies volatility in both directions, and that sharp daily swings can say more about positioning than about fundamentals.
93b5534af2ec.summary: Bitcoin recovered above $63,000 following a selloff driven by liquidations, Investing.com reported. The rebound shows how forced selling can exaggerate swings in both directions.
93b5534af2ec.pixel_take: Leveraged traders got a lesson in gravity, then bitcoin remembered it has a trampoline. Borrowed conviction, it turns out, is the most fragile kind.
93b5534af2ec.why_it_matters: Liquidation-driven moves show how much leverage shapes crypto prices, so headline swings may reflect forced trades rather than new fundamentals. For investors, that means volatility risk is real, especially when borrowing is involved.

The preceding selloff was driven by liquidations.
Forced selling from leveraged bets can magnify moves both ways.

b29106e08869.headline: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO and Stocks Jump, With Wall Street Already Halfway to Cheerful
body: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, and the news sent the chipmaker's shares soaring on Monday, according to The New York Times. The announcement landed as U.S. markets were already leaning higher.

Before the Nvidia headline, the S&P 500 was set to rise on Monday, recovering from a sharp fall the week before. In other words, the market had already put on its good shoes, and the Huang news handed it a jetpack.

The material available does not explain the circumstances of Mr. Huang's departure or the reasons for his return, so those details remain unclear. What is clear is the reaction: investors treated the reinstatement as good news for Nvidia, and the stock moved sharply on it.

The reaction shows how closely a company's valuation can be tied to its leader. Nvidia is one of the most closely watched companies in the market, and a founder-style chief executive often carries a premium in investors' minds. When leadership looks uncertain, shares tend to reflect that. When certainty returns, they can rebound quickly.

It also matters beyond one company. Large, heavily weighted stocks can move major indexes like the S&P 500, so a big swing in Nvidia can ripple into retirement accounts, index funds and the broader mood on Wall Street. Monday's rise followed a rough prior week, and the Nvidia news added momentum to a market already trying to recover.

163a5367dcf2.headline: China Says It Swapped a Damaged Oil Well Casing Nearly 6,000 Feet Down, a Claimed Record
body: Xinjiang Oilfield, a unit of China National Petroleum Corp. (CNPC), says it has replaced a damaged well casing at a depth of nearly 6,000 feet, a feat it describes as a record, according to Interesting Engineering.

The details are thin. The source material available to us includes the headline and a short teaser, but no technical specifics on how the repair was carried out, how long it took, or what it cost. We also cannot independently verify the record claim, so it should be read as the company's own description.

For non-specialists, a casing is the steel pipe lining an oil well. It keeps the borehole from collapsing, seals off different rock layers and stops fluids from leaking where they shouldn't. When it gets damaged, the usual options are costly: patch it, plug the well, or drill a new one.

Swapping out a casing section at depth, rather than abandoning the well, is the kind of work that can extend the life of an aging field. If the claim holds up, it suggests Chinese operators are pushing workover technology, the repair and maintenance side of the oil business that rarely makes headlines but matters a lot to margins.

Neither the source text nor the teaser says whether the technique will be used more widely or offered commercially. Until CNPC or independent experts provide more detail, the record remains an announcement rather than a verified benchmark.

163a5367dcf2.why_it_matters: Repairing old wells instead of drilling new ones can cut costs and keep output flowing from mature fields. For energy markets, small gains in well longevity add up across thousands of wells. It also shows where national oil companies are investing engineering effort.

9ae3fa8ff2a7.headline: AirPods Pro 3 hit $149, the same price as the weaker AirPods 5
body: Apple's AirPods Pro 3 have fallen to $149 at Amazon and Walmart as of Monday morning, according to The Verge. That is $100 below the $249 list price, a 40 percent discount, and it lands just ahead of Black Friday.

The Verge says it is the lowest price yet for Apple's newest flagship earbuds. They have usually sold for around $199 outside big deal events, and the previous best the outlet had tracked was $169, which is what Best Buy currently charges.

The odd part is the lineup. At $149, the Pro 3 cost the same as the newer AirPods 5 with the wireless charging case, which The Verge calls less impressive. In other words, the premium model is temporarily priced like the budget-minded one.

On features, The Verge describes the Pro 3 as Apple's best-sounding and longest-lasting AirPods, and they come with five silicone ear tips. Compared with the second-generation AirPods Pro, they offer better water resistance (IP57 versus IP54) and longer battery life per charge (eight hours versus six). Noise cancellation is improved too, and built-in sensors can track heart rate. The case also carries Apple's second-generation Ultra Wideband chip.

Prices at big retailers can move quickly during sales season, and the $149 figure applies to the retailers named above. If you were eyeing either pair, the Pro 3 look like the stronger buy at this price, per The Verge.
9ae3fa8ff2a7.summary: The AirPods Pro 3 dropped to $149 at Amazon and Walmart, 40 percent off their $249 list price. That matches the price of the AirPods 5, a less capable model, according to The Verge.
9ae3fa8ff2a7.pixel_take: Apple's pricing ladder just tripped: the fancy earbuds now cost the same as the lesser ones. Black Friday, where the premium seat gets sold at economy fares.
9ae3fa8ff2a7.why_it_matters: Early Black Friday cuts on flagship gadgets show how aggressively retailers compete for holiday spending. When a premium product matches a cheaper model's price, shoppers get more for the same money, and the cheaper model may be pressured to follow.
key_points: AirPods Pro 3 are $149 at Amazon and Walmart, down from $249.
Best Buy sells them for $169, the previous lowest price The Verge had seen.
At $149 they match the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case.

The report, based on a teaser of the story, says the president will push back on the governor's move. The full text of his planned comments was not available, so the specific arguments he intends to make are not yet clear.

The setting is notable. The Justice Department is the federal government's top law enforcement body, and choosing it as the venue signals that the administration wants to frame the issue as a matter of crime and punishment, not just a state-level policy dispute.

The clash also adds another chapter to the long-running political sparring between Trump and Newsom, two high-profile figures from opposing parties. Capital punishment has long been a divisive issue in American politics, with supporters pointing to accountability for the worst crimes and opponents citing cost, error risk and moral concerns.

Commutation is a power governors hold to reduce a sentence without erasing a conviction. In general terms, it means inmates who had been condemned would no longer face execution, though the specifics of their new sentences were not detailed in the material available.

Why does this tension matter beyond Israel? Any renewed strikes involving Iran tend to ripple outward, because the region is central to energy supply and global risk sentiment.
