His biographer Stephen Witt told the BBC that Huang is a visionary on the level of Steve Jobs, but also described a level of arrogance and self-deception, and noted that Huang worked hard to cultivate a family-man image.
7ee65d1ae7eb.summary: Nvidia's board has brought back Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned over two alleged affairs, one involving a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset.
7ee65d1ae7eb.pixel_take: Eleven days: barely enough time for a leather jacket to go out of style, and a board to discover that firing the AI chip king is bad for business.
7ee65d1ae7eb.why_it_matters: Nvidia's chips underpin the AI boom, so who runs the company matters to markets, partners and anyone with tech stocks in their portfolio. The episode shows how key-person risk and geopolitical sensitivities around China can shake even a giant firm within days.
key_points: Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO 11 days after resigning over two alleged affairs.
US officials allege one woman involved is a Chinese intelligence asset; Huang admitted infidelity and apologised.
His estimated fortune fell from nearly $200bn to about $105bn, per Bloomberg.

264c5cfe8be2.headline: Plaud Note Pro AI Recorder Drops to $149.99, So Your Notes Can Finally Take Themselves
body: Plaud's flagship Note Pro AI note taker is on sale for $149.99 from November 19 through November 30, according to Digital Trends. The 20% cut comes off a usual $189 price, and the deal is available directly from Plaud or on Amazon.

The pitch is simple: software bots can handle Zoom, but they go quiet during phone calls and in-person briefings. The Note Pro is dedicated hardware that attaches magnetically to the back of a smartphone using an included case or ring. It is an aluminum slab about the size of a credit card, 0.12 inches thick and 1.06 ounces, with a 0.95-inch AMOLED screen for checking battery and recording status.

On audio, it combines four microphones with a vibration sensor, offering a 16.4-foot pickup range with AI beamforming and noise suppression. A dual-mode system reportedly detects whether you are on a call or in a room and switches automatically. It has 64GB of storage and up to 30 hours of recording in Enhance mode, or 50 hours in Endurance mode.

The software side matters as much. Plaud Agent turns transcripts, highlights and notes into emails, reports, spreadsheets or presentations, and connects with Google Calendar, Slack, Notion and Linear. Plaud Desktop covers online meetings.
The Starter Plan includes 300 free AI transcription minutes per month. Plaud says it meets SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR and EN 18031 standards and does not train AI models on user data unless people opt in.
As always with limited-time deals, the clock is the catch: the promo ends November 30, and Digital Trends frames it as a rare break on flagship productivity hardware.
264c5cfe8be2.summary: Plaud's flagship Note Pro AI recorder is 20% off at $149.99 through November 30 on Plaud's store and Amazon, down from $189, according to Digital Trends.
264c5cfe8be2.pixel_take: A recorder that listens, transcribes and drafts the follow-up email. Meetings that could have been emails are now emails that write themselves about meetings.
264c5cfe8be2.why_it_matters: AI note-taking is moving from software bots to dedicated hardware, and subscriptions plus a one-time device price shape the real cost. For professionals, a $40 saving is small, but it lowers the entry price of a growing gadget category.
key_points: Note Pro costs $149.99 from Nov 19 to Nov 30, versus $189 usually.
It records calls and in-person talks with four microphones and a vibration sensor.
Starter Plan includes 300 free transcription minutes monthly.

30f1434d7064.headline: Amazon Lists Moto Tag 3 Before Motorola Announces It, and It Looks a Lot Like the Tag 2
body: Motorola's Moto Tag 3 has turned up for sale on Amazon before the company has said a word about it, according to The Verge. The Amazon UK listing has reportedly been live since Friday, just five months after the Moto Tag 2 went on sale in the US.

The listing was spotted by X user @matteventu. It shows the tracker in a "Pantone Lucent White" finish for £24.96 (about $33), with a shipping estimate of one to four months. That is less a delivery window than a season of the year.

Leaker Evan Blass shared a second image showing a purple version, described as "Pantone Indigo Blue" on a separate Amazon Italy listing. Both colors are new: the Moto Tag 2 is currently sold only in orange or a grey-ish beige.

The catch is that the Tag 3 doesn't seem very new. According to The Verge, both trackers use a replaceable CR2032 battery, claim more than 500 days of battery life, and support UWB in Android Find Hub. The model number on the back of the Tag 3 images, XT2561-1, also matches the Tag 2's.

That raises the possibility that the "3" is a labeling slip and these are simply new colors of the Tag 2. Motorola hasn't confirmed either way. The Verge has asked the company for clarification and says it will update the story if it responds.
30f1434d7064.summary: A Moto Tag 3 listing appeared on Amazon UK before any announcement, priced at £24.96. Specs and model number match the Moto Tag 2, so it may just be new colors.
30f1434d7064.pixel_take: Motorola's tracker has already been found by the internet before its own announcement. Irony aside, it may just be the old tag in a fresh Pantone outfit.
30f1434d7064.why_it_matters: Cheap item trackers are a competitive niche, and retailer leaks often reveal product plans before companies do. For shoppers, the episode is a reminder to check specs before paying for a higher version number that may just be a new color.
key_points: Moto Tag 3 appeared on Amazon UK at £24.96 (about $33) before any announcement.
New Pantone colors are the only clear difference from the Moto Tag 2.
Matching battery, UWB support and model number suggest it could be a mislabeled Tag 2.

6a16b32fcddc.headline: Leaked Russian Records Show Over 1,000 Military Suicides in Ukraine War, and Likely Far More
body: More than 1,000 Russian service members have died by suicide since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, according to an analysis by The Guardian of confidential data from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat. The figures come from a leaked cache of more than 11m death certificates.

The Guardian identified 1,087 suicides among military personnel. At least 614 occurred in occupied parts of Ukraine or in Russian border regions, mainly Belgorod and Bryansk. A further 885 deaths in or near Ukraine were logged as firearm injuries of "undetermined intent", a category experts say can hide suicides. Together, the suicides add up to roughly a regiment of dead.

The records show a steady climb: more than 50 in 2022, more than 200 in 2024, a peak of 365 in 2025, and almost 300 already in 2026 despite incomplete records. Of the suicides in the war zone, 43 involved soldiers aged 18 or 19. The data also includes 108 men under 25 who died away from the front, some probably conscripts pressed into signing contracts that allow deployment.

Analysts say the true toll is higher. Ivan Chuvilyaev of Idite Lesom, a group that helps soldiers desert, called the numbers a low estimate and said reports are simply passed up the chain. He and military analyst Rob Lee noted that soldiers who kill themselves on the battlefield, for example when wounded or as a drone approaches, would likely be recorded as combat deaths.

The Guardian cited cases where families were told one thing and records showed another. Lt Col Sergei Savenok's wife was told his death was suicide, yet his certificate lists an undetermined firearm injury. Private Alexander Lazor's family was told he died in combat, but two comrades said their unit was told he took his own life.

Lee pointed to coercion, abuse and fear of dangerous missions inside the Russian army. The Kremlin does not publish military suicide data and treats casualty figures as a state secret. Mediazona reported 20,662 men facing military court cases for refusing to serve by the end of May 2025, and IStories found at least 49,000 servicemen declared deserters or absent without leave.
6a16b32fcddc.summary: Leaked Rosstat data analysed by The Guardian records over 1,000 suicides among Russian military personnel since the invasion of Ukraine, with experts saying the real figure is almost certainly higher.
6a16b32fcddc.why_it_matters: The data offers a rare window into morale and losses inside Russia's army, which the Kremlin treats as secret. Hidden strain on manpower and discipline matters for how long Russia can sustain the war, and for sanctions, energy and market risk tied to it.
key_points: Guardian found 1,087 military suicides in leaked Rosstat data, plus 885 "undetermined intent" firearm deaths near Ukraine.
Recorded suicides rose from over 50 in 2022 to 365 in 2025, with almost 300 already in 2026.
Experts and activists say the real toll is higher because many cases are likely recorded as combat deaths.

0c873259805e.headline: Quantum computers could one day come for $72 billion in ETH, researchers warn, and they have a fix
body: Researchers say Ethereum wallets holding roughly $72 billion worth of ether could be exposed to a future quantum attack, according to a CoinDesk report published on November 23, 2026. The at-risk accounts are those whose public keys are visible on the blockchain.

According to the findings, these accounts hold nearly 55% of all ether that is not locked up in staking. That makes the issue less an obscure corner case and more a question about where most of the network's liquid wealth is sitting.

The concern rests on a well-known idea in cryptography: a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could, in theory, work backward from a visible public key to the private key that controls the funds. Accounts that have exposed their public keys give a would-be attacker a head start. No such machine is described in the material as existing today, so this is a warning about the future rather than a live theft.

The researchers did not stop at the alarm bell. They propose a way to migrate these accounts to quantum-resistant security, which would let holders move to newer protections before the threat becomes practical. The teaser does not detail how the proposal works, so the specifics remain to be seen.

The story highlights a broader challenge for crypto: blockchains are built to be hard to change, yet security assumptions can age. Upgrading a network with this much value at stake takes coordination among developers, wallet providers and ordinary holders, and that kind of herding is famously slower than any quantum processor.
0c873259805e.summary: Researchers say Ethereum accounts with visible public keys hold about $72 billion in ETH, nearly 55% of non-staked supply, and could be vulnerable to future quantum attacks. They propose migrating to quantum-resistant security.
0c873259805e.pixel_take: Quantum computers may someday crack wallets like piñatas, so the researchers are suggesting we swap the candy for a vault first. Getting everyone to actually move, though, is the real puzzle.
0c873259805e.why_it_matters: Nearly 55% of non-staked ether sits in accounts that could be targeted if quantum computing advances, so the issue touches the security assumptions behind a huge pool of value. Investors and developers will be watching whether a migration plan gains traction well before any real threat arrives.
key_points: Accounts with visible public keys hold about $72 billion in ETH.
They represent nearly 55% of ether outside staking.
Researchers propose moving them to quantum-resistant security.

aaf0595a93ae.headline: Carney shares a stage with Trump and Carney impersonators at Ottawa press dinner
body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney took the stage on Saturday at the annual Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner in Ottawa alongside two impersonators: one playing himself and one playing U.S. President Donald Trump, according to The Hill.

The Hill's report says Carney announced he was "pressing the…" before the teaser cuts off, and the full text of the remark was not available to us. The headline's "Fake news" line is a nod to the evening's comedic tone, though the material does not say who delivered it or in what context.

The Press Gallery dinner is a long-running tradition in which politicians and journalists set aside their usual sparring for an evening of roasting each other. Self-deprecating humor from the guest of honor is part of the script, and bringing along a double of yourself and of the leader of your largest trading partner is a fairly bold way to follow it.

The setting is notable given how central Trump has been to Canadian politics. Canada and the United States are deeply intertwined economically, and Canadian leaders have spent considerable energy managing that relationship. Humor at a media dinner is not policy, but it offers a glimpse of how a prime minister chooses to talk about a sensitive neighbor in public.

Since the full account of the performance is not available, details of the jokes and the audience reaction remain unclear. What is confirmed is the basic scene: a prime minister, two lookalikes, and a room full of journalists in Ottawa.
aaf0595a93ae.summary: Canadian PM Mark Carney shared the stage with impersonators of himself and Donald Trump at Ottawa's Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner on Saturday, according to The Hill.
aaf0595a93ae.pixel_take: Two impersonators on one stage, and Ottawa still had a hard time deciding which Carney was the real one. At least the trade talks have better lighting this way.
aaf0595a93ae.why_it_matters: Canada's relationship with the U.S. shapes trade, markets and the Canadian dollar, so how its leader publicly frames Trump gets attention. A comedy dinner is no policy shift, but tone between the two governments can color the mood around negotiations.
key_points: Carney appeared with impersonators of himself and Trump at the Press Gallery dinner in Ottawa.
The event took place Saturday, per The Hill.
Full details of the jokes were not available in the source material.

a19cafb4c3cc.headline: Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia, Stocks Are Surging, and Wall Street Wonders: Can the Party Last?
body: MarketWatch reported on Monday, November 23, 2026, that the stock market is surging as Nvidia's Jensen Huang returns to the spotlight, and it asked whether the rally can last through Thanksgiving week.

The piece, a weekly markets roundup, points readers to the AI-related earnings coming up in the holiday-shortened week. With Nvidia at the center of the artificial-intelligence trade, investors tend to treat results from companies tied to AI spending as a gauge of whether the boom still has legs.

The teaser also flags a few other items. One is the argument that memory stocks look cheap. Another is how much less drivers will pay at the pump. The last is a $100,000 pottery-studio dilemma, which is a reminder that not every money question involves a trillion-dollar chip giant.

As general context, holiday weeks often bring thinner trading volumes, which can make market moves look bigger than they are. Rallies concentrated in a handful of AI-linked names also leave indexes sensitive to any disappointment from those companies.
a19cafb4c3cc.summary: MarketWatch says stocks are surging with Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and asks whether the rally can last through a Thanksgiving week packed with AI earnings, with a look at memory stocks and gas prices.

ae8335cf5c27.headline: Cross River Bank Starts Lending Against Bitcoin, With Loans Up to $250,000
body: Cross River Bank, a US lender, is entering Bitcoin-backed lending, according to Cointelegraph. The bank is offering loans from $10,000 to $250,000 through LendingUSA, letting borrowers get cash while keeping their Bitcoin.

The pitch is simple: instead of selling coins and possibly triggering a tax bill, a holder pledges them as collateral and borrows against them. It is the crypto version of taking out a loan on your house rather than selling the kitchen.

The material available does not specify details such as interest rates, loan-to-value ratios, liquidation terms or when the product becomes available. Those are the things borrowers should check first, because the fine print decides whether this is a handy tool or an expensive surprise.

Crypto-backed lending is not new, but it has a mixed history. Earlier waves of lenders in the sector ran into trouble, which is part of why a bank with a regulated footprint offering such loans through a established consumer lending channel draws attention.

Still, the story as reported is narrow: a bank, a partner, and a loan range. Whether it signals a broader move by traditional lenders toward digital assets as collateral will depend on how the product performs and how many other banks follow.
ae8335cf5c27.summary: Cross River Bank is offering Bitcoin-backed loans of $10,000 to $250,000 through LendingUSA, letting borrowers access cash without selling their Bitcoin, according to Cointelegraph.
ae8335cf5c27.pixel_take: Bitcoin holders can now say they're not selling, just borrowing very hard against their conviction. The bank, meanwhile, gets to hold the digital rock.
ae8335cf5c27.why_it_matters: Borrowing against Bitcoin lets holders raise cash without selling, which can matter for investment strategy and taxes. A bank entering the space suggests crypto is edging further into mainstream finance, though borrowers still face price-swing risk on their collateral.
key_points: Cross River Bank is offering Bitcoin-backed loans through LendingUSA.
Loans range from $10,000 to $250,000.
Borrowers can access cash without selling their Bitcoin.

body: Gizmodo's Consumer Tech Editor Raymond Wong has published his list of the eight most underrated tech gifts of 2026. The piece went up on November 23, 2026, just as holiday shopping season gets going.

ce3073bd5d64.headline: Russian strikes kill at least 15 in Kyiv region as Ukraine hits Russian oil sites and ships
body: Russian strikes on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people overnight into Monday, according to Ukrainian officials, with rescuers still searching rubble for survivors after a block of flats partially collapsed in the town of Dymer, about 45km north of the capital.

Regional official Tymur Tkachenko said at least 11 people died in the five-storey building in Dymer. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said the dead included a teenager and that 11 people, among them two children, could not be reached. Rescuers have pulled out survivors, including a 79-year-old woman and a child.

Elsewhere, a strike on a supermarket in Vyshneve, just south of Kyiv, killed three people and wounded 15, including three children, Mayor Illya Dikov said. One more person died in Bila Tserkva when a private home was hit and caught fire. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

The attacks come days after Vladimir Putin promised a "much more painful" response to Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge. Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the section used by vehicles and halting train services, according to Al Jazeera. Moscow has also stepped up pressure on Ukraine's energy network as temperatures fall toward freezing.

Ukraine kept up its own campaign. Drones hit oil storage facilities in Russia's Tatarstan region, about 1,000km from the Ukrainian border, along with a petroleum products plant in Rostov and reportedly the city of Perm, home to a large refinery. Russian news agency Interfax reported fires but no immediate casualties.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. He said a second target, the cargo ship MV Angara, was hit, and that a Ka-27 helicopter was destroyed. These claims come from Zelenskyy and were not independently verified in the material.
ce3073bd5d64.summary: Russian strikes killed at least 15 people in the Kyiv region, mostly in a collapsed apartment block in Dymer. Ukraine reported hitting Russian oil facilities and, per Zelenskyy, sinking a Russian corvette.
ce3073bd5d64.why_it_matters: Attacks on energy infrastructure on both sides feed into oil and power supply risks as winter approaches. Strikes on Russian refineries and storage sites can affect fuel supply and keep energy markets sensitive to the war's escalation.
key_points: At least 15 killed in Kyiv region, including 11 in a collapsed block of flats in Dymer.
Strikes follow Putin's pledge of a 'much more painful' response over Kerch Bridge attacks.
Ukraine hit Russian oil facilities and says it sank a Russian corvette near Libya.

f205e38d2cf7.headline: Marvel's final Avengers: Doomsday trailer packs in nearly every hero, and Doom wants their 'stolen lives' back
body: Marvel has released the final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday, after days of rumors, according to Ars Technica. The film, the penultimate chapter of the MCU's Phase Six and a milestone for the so-called Multiverse Saga, opens in theaters on December 18, 2026.

The footage suggests the Avengers will pay for tampering with the timeline to undo the blip in Endgame. Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom tells the assembled heroes that all of them have lived stolen lives, and that they must now give them back.

The story is set 14 months after Thunderbolts*. The official logline promises heroes from three universes on a deadly collision course: Earth-616 (the Avengers, Wakandans and New Avengers), Earth-828 (the Fantastic Four) and the original X-Men. The cast list includes Chris Hemsworth, Anthony Mackie, Pedro Pascal, Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen and many more, with cameos expected from the likes of Tom Holland and Benedict Cumberbatch.

Chris Evans' Steve Rogers gets a big role. The trailer opens with him and Peggy Carter agreeing they made the right choice, though Steve feels guilty about keeping the truth from their teenage son. We also learn that the couple built their life in the same alternate universe as the Fantastic Four, who show up to recruit him. Most of the rest is previously seen footage, plus new moments such as Cyclops facing Doom and several Sentinels, and Thor grumbling that he doesn't know who half the group is.

Wanda Maximoff doesn't appear, though she may be among three Latverian witches who briefly show up. Ars Technica says it's unclear whether the film will match Infinity War and Endgame, but it should be a spectacle.
The release date sets up a box-office showdown: Dune: Part III opens the same day. Avengers: Secret Wars, due December 17, 2027, will close out Phase Six.
f205e38d2cf7.summary: Marvel's final Avengers: Doomsday trailer crams in heroes from three universes and hints Doctor Doom blames the Avengers for 'stolen lives.' The film opens December 18, 2026, against Dune: Part III.
f205e38d2cf7.pixel_take: Marvel's casting strategy appears to be 'yes.' Thor admits he doesn't know half the team, which makes him the audience, and also the person who needs a spreadsheet.
f205e38d2cf7.why_it_matters: Big franchise tentpoles move studio fortunes and theater traffic, and a head-to-head opening against Dune: Part III makes this a closely watched box-office clash. Marketing at this scale shows how heavily studios lean on established intellectual property to draw audiences.
key_points: Final Doomsday trailer features heroes from three universes, with Doctor Doom accusing them of living 'stolen lives.'
Steve Rogers is central, living in the same alternate universe as the Fantastic Four.
The film opens December 18, 2026, the same day as Dune: Part III.

66a36c3ad63d.headline: Trump reportedly backed off firing Lutnick after a big donation, Haberman says
body: New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman said on Sunday that President Trump stepped back from firing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick after Lutnick made a significant donation to the president, according to The Hill.

The Hill's report, based on Haberman's comments, also says Trump complained about the attention being paid to Lutnick's sons. The teaser cuts off there, so the full context of that remark is not available.

The material does not say how large the donation was, when it was made, who received it, or what prompted the talk of a firing. Those details matter, and readers should treat the claim with care until more reporting fills them in. The White House response is also not included in the material we have.

Context helps here. Cabinet secretaries serve at the president's pleasure, and the Commerce Department sits at the center of tariffs, trade policy and export controls. Any hint that a job might be tied to money, rather than performance, tends to draw scrutiny from ethics watchdogs and political opponents.

For now, this is a secondhand account of a journalist's reporting, not a documented finding. Whether it grows into a bigger story will depend on confirmation, on-the-record responses and any further details about the donation.
66a36c3ad63d.summary: NYT journalist Maggie Haberman said Trump backed off firing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick after a significant donation, per The Hill. Key details, including the amount, remain unreported.
66a36c3ad63d.pixel_take: Nothing says job security like a well-timed check. Washington's oldest performance review remains undefeated, though the details here are still thin.
66a36c3ad63d.why_it_matters: The Commerce Secretary helps shape tariffs and trade policy, which move markets and prices. Claims that money influenced a personnel decision raise questions about how those choices are made. Investors and businesses watch the department's stability closely.
key_points: Maggie Haberman said Trump backed off firing Howard Lutnick after a significant donation.
Trump also reportedly complained about attention on Lutnick's sons.
Donation size, timing and White House response are not in the available material.

1faafad57fc7.headline: Mr. Huang Resigns From Nvidia After Extramarital Relationships Come to Light, NYT Reports
body: A person identified only as Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, according to a teaser published by The New York Times on Nov. 23, 2026.

e5dc49b860e0.headline: Bitrue's AI Sees XRP Echoing November 2022, Before Next Year's Rally
body: Crypto exchange Bitrue says its AI analysis has found that XRP is currently showing patterns similar to those seen in November 2022, a period that came before a rally the following year, according to an Investing.com headline published on November 23, 2026.

That is essentially all the material tells us. The original article text was not available, so details such as the specific indicators compared, price levels, timeframes or any forecast are not known and are not reported here.

Still, the framing is familiar to anyone who has spent time around crypto markets. Pattern-matching against past cycles is a popular genre of analysis: find a stretch of history that looks like today, note what happened next, and suggest history may rhyme. Adding an AI label gives the exercise a modern gloss, though the underlying logic is still comparing charts across time.

The caveat is the usual one. Similarity to an earlier period does not guarantee the same outcome, since markets are shaped by regulation, liquidity, investor sentiment and events that no past chart can anticipate. An analysis from an exchange also comes from a company with a stake in trading activity, so readers should treat it as one input rather than a prediction.

For now, the takeaway is modest: a crypto platform says an AI tool sees a resemblance between XRP today and late 2022. Whether that resemblance means anything for the next move is a question only the market can answer.
e5dc49b860e0.summary: Bitrue says its AI analysis finds XRP showing patterns like those of November 2022, which preceded a rally the next year, per Investing.com. Details were not available, and such comparisons are no guarantee.
e5dc49b860e0.pixel_take: An AI says XRP's chart looks like 2022's. Markets love a rerun, but they have a habit of changing the ending without telling the audience.
e5dc49b860e0.why_it_matters: Historical pattern comparisons often influence crypto sentiment and trading decisions, even though they are not reliable predictors. Investors should weigh exchange-published analysis carefully, since it is not independent advice and past price behavior does not guarantee future results.
key_points: Bitrue's AI reportedly finds XRP resembling November 2022.
That period was followed by a rally the next year, per the headline.
Specific data and forecasts were not available, and past patterns guarantee nothing.

b415f7b32fd8.headline: Idaho Record Collector Slips On Boxing Gloves, Hurls Medicine Ball Into the Guinness Books
body: An Idaho man who holds more simultaneous Guinness World Records titles than anyone else has added another to his collection, this time by throwing a medicine ball while wearing boxing gloves, according to UPI.

The headline on the report refers to men, plural, wearing gloves and breaking the record, but the material available gives few details beyond that. The teaser does not say how far the ball traveled, how heavy it was, or when and where the attempt happened, so we will not guess at any of those numbers.

What we do know is the identity of the star: the Idaho man is described as the person with the most concurrent Guinness World Records titles. That means he holds a large number of records at the same moment, which is a bit like being the landlord of the record book.

The challenge itself has a certain absurd elegance. A medicine ball is a weighted ball normally gripped in both hands for workouts. Boxing gloves are designed for punching, not for holding things. Combine them and a simple throw becomes a test of grip, technique and stubbornness.

Guinness World Records has long welcomed quirky twists on ordinary activities, and this one fits the pattern: take a familiar motion, add an awkward handicap, and see how far human determination can stretch. UPI published video of the feat.
b415f7b32fd8.summary: An Idaho man with the most concurrent Guinness World Records titles added another by throwing a medicine ball while wearing boxing gloves, UPI reports. Video of the feat accompanied the story.
b415f7b32fd8.pixel_take: Holding a medicine ball in boxing gloves is hard enough. Doing it as the reigning king of simultaneous records suggests his trophy shelf needs its own zip code.
b415f7b32fd8.why_it_matters: This one is not moving markets, but it shows how record attempts keep turning ordinary gym gear into attention-grabbing content. Viral stunts like this feed the media and brand ecosystem that Guinness and online video thrive on.
key_points: An Idaho man holds the most concurrent Guinness World Records titles.
His newest title came from throwing a medicine ball while wearing boxing gloves.
UPI reported the feat; distance and ball weight were not given in the material.

17dae86ddff9.headline: Blade Runner 2099 Lands on Prime Video With Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer
body: Prime Video is adding a new chapter to the Blade Runner universe. According to Gizmodo, the limited series Blade Runner 2099 arrives on November 25 and stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer.

The material we have is short, so details on the plot, the number of episodes and the creative team are not available here. What is clear is the format: a limited series, meaning a defined story with a beginning and an end rather than an open-ended run of seasons.
Gizmodo describes the show as a gripping new chapter for the sci-fi franchise. That is the outlet's assessment, and viewers will get to judge for themselves once the series is streaming.

Franchise revivals are a familiar play for streamers. An established name comes with built-in awareness, which helps a new show stand out in a crowded catalog, and a limited-series format keeps the commitment contained for both the studio and the audience.
17dae86ddff9.summary: Prime Video's limited series Blade Runner 2099, starring Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer, premieres November 25, extending the sci-fi franchise, according to Gizmodo.
17dae86ddff9.pixel_take: Streaming services keep digging up beloved sci-fi worlds, and honestly, a limited series at least promises an ending. In this economy, that's practically a luxury.
17dae86ddff9.why_it_matters: Streamers lean on established franchises to attract and retain subscribers, and big-name releases like this are part of how they compete for your monthly subscription money. A limited series also gives viewers a defined commitment instead of an open-ended one.
key_points: Blade Runner 2099 is a limited series on Prime Video.
It premieres November 25 and stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer.
Gizmodo calls it a gripping new chapter for the franchise.

c2ee55235eac.headline: ECB Preps to Take Tokenized Securities as Collateral, Targeting June 2027
body: The European Central Bank plans to let banks pledge more tokenized securities as collateral, according to Cointelegraph. The aim is to start accepting securities issued on platforms licensed under the EU's distributed ledger pilot program in June 2027.

In plain terms, collateral is the stuff banks hand over to the central bank in exchange for funding. Until now, that pile has mostly consisted of traditional assets sitting in traditional systems. The ECB's plan would widen the door to securities that are born and recorded on blockchain-style infrastructure, as long as they come from platforms that hold a license under the EU pilot regime.

That license condition matters. The plan does not appear to be a free-for-all for any digital token with a ticker and a dream. It points only to securities issued on venues that regulators have already approved under the distributed ledger pilot program, which is designed as a controlled testing ground for this technology.

The source material gives only the headline and the target date, so details such as eligibility criteria, haircuts or which specific platforms might qualify are not available here. The June 2027 timing is described as an aim, not a done deal, so the schedule could still shift.

Even so, the direction is clear: a major central bank is signaling that tokenized assets can be part of the plumbing of regular monetary operations, not just a side experiment. For banks and market infrastructure firms building on distributed ledgers, that is a meaningful vote of confidence.
c2ee55235eac.summary: The ECB aims to begin accepting securities issued on platforms licensed under the EU's distributed ledger pilot as collateral in June 2027, according to Cointelegraph, widening the role of tokenized assets.
c2ee55235eac.pixel_take: The ECB is telling tokenized securities they can finally sit at the grown-ups' table, provided they show a license at the door and wait until June 2027.
c2ee55235eac.why_it_matters: Central bank acceptance makes tokenized securities more useful, since assets that can be pledged for funding are more attractive to hold and issue. It could encourage banks and platforms to invest in blockchain-based market infrastructure across Europe.
key_points: The ECB aims to accept more tokenized securities as collateral starting June 2027.
Eligible securities would be issued on platforms licensed under the EU's distributed ledger pilot program.
Details like criteria and haircuts were not included in the available material.

4f474af5544e.headline: Alienware's 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor drops to $280, its lowest price yet
body: Alienware's AW2726DM, a 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor, is on sale for $279.99 at Best Buy and Dell ahead of Black Friday, according to The Verge. That is $70 below its original $349.99 price and the lowest it has been so far.

The panel runs at 1440p resolution with a 240Hz refresh rate. The Verge's reviewer bought one at launch and has used it for both work and play for several months, calling it a monitor that looks and performs like one costing hundreds more.

The appeal comes from the QD-OLED technology. It delivers strong contrast, deep blacks and fine control over brightness, things that cheaper panel types struggle to match. The 240Hz refresh rate also gives a graphics card plenty of room to push fast frames in PC games, and the monitor works well with consoles too.

Connectivity is covered by HDMI and DisplayPort inputs. The one notable flaw the reviewer points to is the lack of USB-C video support, which could matter if you want to connect a laptop with a single cable.

According to the reviewer, the monitor still holds up against newer models and had more features than similarly priced rivals at launch. The Verge suggests it as a holiday gift for yourself or the gamer in your life. As the outlet notes, it may earn a commission on purchases made through its links.
4f474af5544e.summary: Alienware's 27-inch 1440p 240Hz QD-OLED AW2726DM is $279.99 at Best Buy and Dell, down from $349.99, according to The Verge. It is the monitor's lowest price yet.
4f474af5544e.pixel_take: OLED contrast used to cost a small fortune. Now it costs less than many wallets expect on Black Friday, and the only thing missing is USB-C video.
4f474af5544e.why_it_matters: OLED gaming monitors have long carried a hefty premium, and a sub-$300 QD-OLED shows how fast that premium is shrinking. For shoppers, holiday sales on last-generation hardware can deliver the best value per dollar.
key_points: The AW2726DM is $279.99 at Best Buy and Dell, down $70 from $349.99.
It is a 27-inch 1440p QD-OLED panel with a 240Hz refresh rate.
Its main flaw is the lack of USB-C video support.

48ebf8f03916.headline: Report Says Gaza Is a 'Toxic Wasteland', With Contamination Across 99% of Its Territory
body: A new study says Israel's war has left toxic contamination across 99% of Gaza's territory, according to Al Jazeera's report on the findings. The pollution includes heavy metals, explosive residues and biological hazards.

The report warns that these contaminants threaten the health of Palestinians and the local environment for decades. The material available does not give details on how the study was conducted or who carried it out, so those points remain unclear.

Heavy metals and explosive residues are the kind of pollutants that do not simply disappear once the fighting stops. They can linger in soil and water, and can enter the food chain. Biological hazards, which typically come from damaged sanitation and unburied waste, add a separate public health risk.

The scale of the figure, 99% of the territory, suggests that contamination is not confined to a few hot spots. Any future cleanup would therefore have to be vast, and that matters for planning reconstruction.

Environmental remediation of this kind is expensive and slow, and it usually requires specialist equipment, expertise and long-term funding. Those needs will weigh on any plan for rebuilding housing, farmland, water systems and other infrastructure in Gaza.
This article is based on a summary of the report's headline findings. Further detail on methods, specific pollutants and recommendations was not available in the material reviewed.
48ebf8f03916.summary: A new report says toxic contamination, including heavy metals, explosive residues and biological hazards, covers 99% of Gaza, threatening health and the environment for decades, according to Al Jazeera.
48ebf8f03916.why_it_matters: Contamination on this scale could add major cost and delay to any reconstruction of Gaza, since land and water would need cleanup before rebuilding. It also raises long-term health burdens and questions about who will fund remediation.
key_points: A new study finds toxic contamination across 99% of Gaza's territory.
Pollutants include heavy metals, explosive residues and biological hazards.
The report warns of health and environmental threats lasting decades.

5d73a5474c02.headline: Sen.-elect Flanagan says Americans outside the Beltway know things are 'on fire'
body: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, said Sunday that the federal government is not doing enough to tackle the problems facing everyday Americans, according to The Hill. Her blunt remark about people outside the Beltway, which the outlet printed with the expletive partly masked, was that they 'understand that s--- is on fire.'

Flanagan also spoke about the incoming group of new senators, describing the class as diverse in lived experience and in geography, according to The Hill's teaser. The full context of her comments was not available, so it is unclear which specific policies or officials she had in mind.

The framing is a familiar one in politics: the idea that Washington is out of touch with kitchen-table concerns while the rest of the country is dealing with the consequences. Newly elected lawmakers often use that contrast to signal they plan to shake things up, and to set themselves apart from the institution they are about to join.

Whether the rhetoric turns into action is the open question. A freshman senator has limited power on her own, and the Senate's rules and narrow margins tend to slow even popular ideas. Still, the comments offer an early look at the tone Flanagan intends to bring to the chamber.
5d73a5474c02.summary: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) said Sunday that the federal government isn't effectively addressing everyday Americans' problems, arguing people outside Washington know things are 'on fire,' according to The Hill.
5d73a5474c02.pixel_take: Nothing says 'welcome to the Senate' like announcing the building is on fire before you've even found the cafeteria. At least she's bringing her own smoke alarm.
5d73a5474c02.why_it_matters: Messaging from incoming lawmakers hints at the legislative priorities that can shape budgets, taxes and regulation. Voters and markets watch for whether cost-of-living frustration turns into concrete policy. For now, it is rhetoric, not a plan.
key_points: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) spoke Sunday, per The Hill.
She said the federal government isn't effectively confronting everyday Americans' problems.
She described the incoming Senate class as diverse in experience and geography.

524518cf00bc.headline: HAN CHAIN Sets December 18, 2026 Date for Debut of Flagship Project ARGO
body: HAN CHAIN has scheduled the launch of its first flagship project, called ARGO, for December 18, 2026, according to a headline published by Investing.com on November 23, 2026.

That is essentially everything the available material says. No article text accompanied the headline, so details about what ARGO actually does, who is behind HAN CHAIN, where it will run, or how it will be funded are not available to us, and we are not going to guess.

What we can say is that the announcement follows a familiar playbook in the crypto and blockchain world: a project names a date for its first major product well ahead of time, building anticipation before any technical specifics are tested in public. A date on a calendar is a promise, not a product, and launches in this sector have a long record of shifting.

For readers weighing anything connected to the project, the sensible approach is to wait for primary documents such as official announcements, technical documentation and any independent audits before drawing conclusions. Until then, December 18 is simply a date to watch.
PixelContent will update this story if more information about HAN CHAIN and ARGO becomes available.
524518cf00bc.summary: HAN CHAIN says its first flagship project, ARGO, will launch on December 18, 2026, per Investing.com. No further details about the project were available in the material.
524518cf00bc.pixel_take: A launch date with no details is like a gift box that's all ribbon. December 18 will tell us whether there's anything inside.
524518cf00bc.why_it_matters: Launch announcements in crypto can move attention and sometimes money well before a product exists. With so few details public, readers should treat this as an unverified claim and look for documentation before making any financial decisions.
key_points: HAN CHAIN plans to launch its first flagship project, ARGO, on December 18, 2026.
The news was reported by Investing.com on November 23, 2026.
No details on ARGO's function, backers or technology were available.

6360118ef85d.headline: Next says supplier hack exposed some data, but not yours (so far)
body: Fashion retailer Next has disclosed that some of its data was accessed in a cyber breach at a third-party online supplier, according to BBC News. The company, headquartered in Enderby, Leicestershire, told investors it has found no evidence that customers' personal data was compromised.

Next said one of its suppliers alerted it to the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next". The retailer said it moved immediately to investigate the nature and scope of the breach alongside the supplier.

The company stressed that its investigations are continuing, but said current evidence suggests no customer personal data was affected. It also said the information involved is limited and, on its present assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against customers or Next itself.
Next said it is treating the matter with the utmost seriousness and is working with the supplier, the police and regulators.

The episode adds to a run of retail cyber incidents. In October, Asos said an unauthorised party had gained access to an employee's account, prompting a phone alert to customers saying the retailer had been hacked; the firm said some personal data, including names and contact details, was accessed. In 2025, Marks & Spencer suffered a major cyber-attack that halted all online sales for about six weeks and contributed to some empty shelves in stores.
The Next case is a reminder that a company's security is only as strong as its weakest supplier. Even when a retailer locks its own doors, a vendor with access to its data can leave a window open.
6360118ef85d.summary: Next says a cyber breach at a third-party supplier exposed some of its data, but it has found no evidence that customer personal data was compromised. Investigations continue with police and regulators.
6360118ef85d.pixel_take: Next says the stolen data is 'benign', which is the corporate way of saying the hackers got the digital equivalent of the office stationery cupboard. Still, the supplier's lock apparently needed a closer look.
6360118ef85d.why_it_matters: Retailers increasingly rely on third-party suppliers, which widens the attack surface for hackers and can disrupt sales or shake customer trust. Recent incidents at Asos and M&S show the potential cost, and investors will watch whether Next's early reassurance holds up as the probe continues.
key_points: Next says some of its data was accessed via a breach at a third-party online supplier.
The retailer says there is no evidence customer personal data was compromised and the data cannot be used for fraud.
It is working with the supplier, police and regulators as investigations continue.

1a23a1679977.headline: Boom's supersonic engine core roars to life, but data centers get the first ride
body: Boom Supersonic has successfully fired up the prototype core of its own jet engine, the company said, in a test on November 21 at its site at Colorado Air and Space Port, east of Denver. According to New Atlas, it lit on the second attempt, after CEO Blake Scholl put the odds of success below 50%.

The core, called the Sprint Core, reached 6,500 rpm while nearly 2,000 sensors streamed data, Scholl told Aviation Week. The run was deliberately short, and Boom plans to push it harder over the next couple of months.

It is the heart of two machines. Symphony wraps the core in a fan to produce about 40,000 lb of thrust for Overture, Boom's planned Mach 1.7 airliner. Superpower drops the fan and uses the hot gases to spin a turbine connected to a generator, making a 42-MW gas turbine for AI data centers. The two share more than 75% of their parts, according to Boom.

The company built its own engine because it had to. Rolls-Royce, its partner since 2020, left the project, GE and Safran passed, and Pratt & Whitney said supersonic engines were not in its plans. Boom has 130 orders and pre-orders for Overture from United, American Airlines and Japan Airlines.

The turbines are meant to pay the bills first. Data centers are scrambling for power, and gas turbines are in short supply. Still, Crusoe's order for 29 turbines worth $1.25 billion fell apart in September. Scholl says other customers will receive about 250 MW next year, without naming them. Boom targets 25 turbines a year by 2028 and 50 by 2029, with first deliveries in mid-2027.

The airliner is the shakier part. The official 2029 target is slipping: United CEO Scott Kirby said it will take longer, and Scholl admitted Overture might arrive a year or two late. A full engine test is expected around mid-2027.
1a23a1679977.summary: Boom Supersonic lit its prototype engine core on its second try. The design will power the Overture airliner eventually, but AI data-center turbines come first, while the airliner's 2029 target looks increasingly shaky.
1a23a1679977.pixel_take: Boom's path to Mach 1.7 runs through a data center. To fly faster than sound, first help chatbots think faster than you.
1a23a1679977.why_it_matters: AI's hunger for power has turned gas turbines into scarce goods, and Boom is betting that selling them can fund a supersonic dream. The lost Crusoe deal shows how fragile that bet is for investors and airline partners alike.
key_points: Boom lit its Sprint Core on the second try on November 21, reaching 6,500 rpm.
The core will power both the Overture airliner's Symphony engine and the 42-MW Superpower turbine for data centers.
Superpower deliveries start mid-2027, while Overture's 2029 target is slipping.

3834868d10c4.headline: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Sank Russian Ship Merkury Off Libya, Hit a Second Vessel
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed responsibility for an attack that sank the Russian ship Merkury in a Libyan port, according to Al Jazeera. He also said Ukraine struck a second Russian vessel that was allegedly used to transport weapons.

The claim, if accurate, would mark a notable stretch of the conflict's maritime front: from the Black Sea, where Ukraine has previously targeted Russian naval assets, to a port on the Mediterranean coast of North Africa. The material available does not say when exactly the attacks took place, how they were carried out, or what the ships were carrying.

Zelenskyy's description of the second vessel as allegedly used for moving weapons suggests Kyiv is framing the strikes as targeting Russian logistics rather than warships. The details of that allegation have not been independently verified in the source material, and no response from Moscow or Libyan authorities is included.

Context matters here. Shipping lanes in the Mediterranean carry a large share of global trade, and any new theater of conflict raises questions for insurers, port operators and shipping companies. Incidents involving vessels tied to a country at war can push up war-risk premiums and complicate routes, even when the targeted ships are not commercial cargo carriers.

For now, this is one side's claim, delivered by a head of state. Independent confirmation of the sinking, the second strike and the cargo claims will determine how far the story travels, and how Libya and Russia respond.
3834868d10c4.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine sank the Russian ship Merkury in a Libyan port and struck a second Russian vessel allegedly used to carry weapons, according to Al Jazeera.
3834868d10c4.why_it_matters: A conflict stretching to Mediterranean ports could unsettle shipping and insurance markets that depend on predictable sea lanes. Higher war-risk costs can eventually feed into freight rates and consumer prices, though the scale here is unclear.
key_points: Zelenskyy claims Ukraine sank the Russian ship Merkury in a Libyan port.
He says a second Russian vessel, allegedly used to transport weapons, was also struck.
Details, timing and independent verification are not provided in the source.

705c37d6a969.headline: Bitcoin's Five-Year Return Is Near Zero, and the Fed Is Holding the Remote
body: Bitcoin's return over the past five years has fallen to roughly zero, according to a CoinDesk piece published on November 23, 2026. Its argument: the big stories that once powered the asset are fading, and what remains is the Federal Reserve.

The material available to us is just that headline, so details are thin. The framing is still clear. A holder who bought five years ago and sat tight would have little to show for it, a stark contrast with the explosive gains crypto fans have long pointed to.

The headline suggests the narratives that carried bitcoin through earlier cycles are losing force. We don't have the article's list of which ones, so we won't guess. The point is that stories alone seem to be doing less heavy lifting than before.

That leaves the Fed. Central bank policy shapes interest rates and liquidity, and speculative assets such as bitcoin have often been sensitive to both. Cheaper money tends to help risk assets; tighter money tends to hurt them. If CoinDesk is right, bitcoin now trades more like a macro instrument than a revolution.

The takeaway for investors is a sober one: a five-year window can swallow even a famously volatile asset's gains, and the timing of entry matters enormously. Whether this is a pause or a lasting shift is the question the market will answer, probably with one eye on Fed meetings.
705c37d6a969.summary: CoinDesk says bitcoin's five-year return is close to zero as its big narratives fade, leaving Federal Reserve policy as the main driver of the market's direction.
705c37d6a969.pixel_take: Five years, wild swings, and bitcoin ends up roughly where it started. The digital gold rush turned out to be a very expensive treadmill, with the Fed adjusting the incline.
705c37d6a969.why_it_matters: If bitcoin now moves mostly on Fed policy, it behaves like other rate-sensitive risk assets, which weakens the case for it as an independent hedge. Investors should weigh entry timing and interest-rate expectations as much as any crypto story.
key_points: CoinDesk reports bitcoin's five-year return is nearly zero.
Great narratives behind the asset appear to be fading.
The Federal Reserve is described as what's left driving the outlook.

94b0ee8f5048.headline: Rocky Road: Hundreds Dress as Balboa on Philly's Famous Museum Steps
body: A crowd of people dressed as boxer Rocky Balboa gathered on the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art to mark the 50th anniversary of the classic film "Rocky," according to UPI. The event was staged as a Guinness World Record attempt.

The headline and teaser from UPI give slightly different counts: the headline says 540 people, while the teaser says 570. With only those two lines available, we can't say which figure is right, or whether the record was officially confirmed.

What is clear is the setting. The museum steps are the spot made famous by the film's training scenes, and they have long drawn fans who want to run up them and strike a victorious pose. Turning them into a mass costume party is a fitting way to mark half a century of the movie.

Mass-participation record attempts like this are a popular way for cities, brands and fan communities to grab attention. They cost relatively little, produce shareable images and give a cultural landmark another round of publicity.
UPI published video of the gathering. Details such as how the record was verified, the previous benchmark and who organized the event were not included in the material we have.
94b0ee8f5048.summary: Hundreds of people dressed as Rocky Balboa on the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps for a Guinness World Record attempt marking the film's 50th anniversary. UPI's reported counts differ: 540 and 570.
94b0ee8f5048.pixel_take: Hundreds of Rockys on one staircase: finally, a crowd where everyone can say they went the distance and nobody has to say "Adrian" alone.
94b0ee8f5048.why_it_matters: Landmark-based fan events show how cultural nostalgia still drives tourism, media attention and local business. Anniversaries of big film franchises are reliable marketing moments for cities and brands alike.
key_points: People dressed as Rocky Balboa on the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps for a Guinness World Record attempt.
The event marked the 50th anniversary of the film "Rocky."
UPI's headline says 540 people while its teaser says 570.

e09aa9a8dd80.headline: Nvidia Brings Back Jensen Huang as CEO and Chair 11 Days After He Resigned
body: Nvidia's board voted Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman, effective immediately, just 11 days after he resigned amid multiple scandals, according to Ars Technica.

The board said its decision rested partly on input from senior US government levels, which assured members that his return poses no national security risk. That is a notable claim given the backdrop: Huang admitted an affair with a woman US intelligence sources believe was working as a Chinese spy, and Nvidia faces allegations of subverting export controls meant to keep its chips out of China. Several government departments are still investigating national security, accounting and corporate governance concerns.

President Trump had backed the comeback publicly. On Truth Social he called the reinstatement the correct and proper decision, and on CNBC he said he spoke to the board directly and indirectly. He said Huang did nothing wrong and had shown bad judgement in somewhat unrelated incidents. Losing his brainpower, Trump argued, would be a much bigger threat than the China allegations.

Huang reportedly formed a war room to engineer his return. Prominent tech figures, including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey, publicly offered support after his resignation. The episode echoes Altman's own firing and swift return at OpenAI three years ago, though there the pressure came from employees rather than industry peers.

Markets liked the news. Nvidia shares had fallen roughly 25 percent since the resignation and nearly 50 percent from their October peak, when it was the world's most valuable company. Stock rose about 30 percent in early trading after the announcement.

The board said it has retained independent counsel and formed an independent committee to investigate what it calls a foreign intelligence effort targeting Huang. It also created a National Security and Export Control Committee and is seeking a new chief compliance officer.
e09aa9a8dd80.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman 11 days after he resigned amid scandals. Trump backed the move, and the stock jumped about 30 percent in early trading while investigations continue.
e09aa9a8dd80.pixel_take: Eleven days: barely long enough for a sabbatical, but plenty to resign, lose a quarter of the stock value, and get rehired. Somewhere, a compliance officer job posting just got very interesting.
e09aa9a8dd80.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, so its leadership drama moves markets and tech valuations well beyond one company. Ongoing investigations and export-control questions could still create regulatory risk for investors. The episode also shows how political backing can shape corporate governance.
key_points: Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO and chairman 11 days after his resignation.
Stock rose about 30 percent in early trading after falling roughly 25 percent since he left.
Government investigations continue, and Nvidia created a national security and export control committee.

94bc57470e7f.headline: Raskin's Supreme Court reform push meets an obstacle named Alito, says The Hill
body: An opinion piece from The Hill, published November 23, 2026, argues that Justice Samuel Alito could be the biggest obstacle to Rep. Jamie Raskin's efforts to reform the U.S. Supreme Court. The teaser frames the situation as an irresistible force about to meet an immovable object.

The material available is limited to the headline and that teaser, so the details of Raskin's proposals and of Alito's specific positions are not laid out here. What the framing does make clear is that the piece sees a looming clash between a lawmaker pushing for changes and a sitting justice positioned to resist them.

Some context helps. Supreme Court justices serve for life, and the Court's structure and rules can only be changed through Congress or constitutional amendment, which makes reform a steep political climb. Proposals in this area have long drawn intense debate, and the justices themselves have generally been protective of the Court's independence.

The Hill's headline suggests the contest may be as much about personalities and institutional power as about policy. Whether it becomes a real confrontation will depend on what Congress does next and how the justices respond, neither of which the available material spells out.

For now, treat this as an opinion-driven preview rather than a report of a concrete legislative fight. It is a useful signal of where the political conversation about the Court is heading, but not a record of decisions already made.
94bc57470e7f.summary: A Hill opinion piece says Justice Samuel Alito may be the biggest obstacle to Rep. Jamie Raskin's Supreme Court reform efforts, previewing a clash between a determined lawmaker and a justice with a lifetime seat.
94bc57470e7f.pixel_take: Irresistible force, meet immovable object. One has a legislative agenda; the other has a lifetime appointment. Place your bets, but don't expect a quick result.
94bc57470e7f.why_it_matters: The Supreme Court decides cases that shape business regulation, markets and household finances, so fights over its structure matter beyond politics. Any serious reform effort could change how predictable the legal landscape is for companies and investors.
key_points: The Hill opinion piece names Justice Alito as Raskin's biggest obstacle to Court reform.
The piece frames the matter as an irresistible force meeting an immovable object.
Details of specific proposals were not available in the source material.

81ff11ce30de.headline: Jensen Huang's Return Lifts Wall Street, But Don't Pop the Champagne Yet
body: U.S. stocks have found some relief, and according to MarketWatch, the return of Jensen Huang is a big reason why. The outlet reports the rebound may be only temporary, since investors still face plenty of other worries.

The material available for this story is brief: a headline and a one-line teaser. That means the details behind the rally, including how far stocks moved and what exactly Huang's return involved, are not spelled out here, and we won't guess at them.

What the framing does tell us is how markets work right now. When one prominent figure can be credited with steadying the whole market, it suggests sentiment is fragile and leans heavily on a few big narratives rather than broad, sturdy confidence.

MarketWatch's warning is the classic one for any relief rally: a bounce is not the same as a recovery. Rebounds driven by a single catalyst tend to fade if the underlying concerns stay unresolved, and the outlet says those other problems remain.

For everyday investors, the takeaway is to treat a sharp up-day with some skepticism. Headlines that declare the market 'saved' are often written just before the next worry arrives, so patience and diversification usually beat chasing the mood of the moment.
81ff11ce30de.summary: MarketWatch says Jensen Huang's return has lifted the U.S. stock market for now, but argues the rebound may not last because investors still have plenty of other problems to worry about.
81ff11ce30de.pixel_take: One man's return steadies the entire market. Wall Street's confidence is apparently a group project where one person did all the work, and everyone else is still worried about the grade.
81ff11ce30de.why_it_matters: If a single storyline can swing the market, sentiment is fragile and vulnerable to the next piece of bad news. Anyone with a retirement account or index funds should expect volatility rather than assume a smooth recovery.
key_points: MarketWatch credits Jensen Huang's return with rescuing U.S. stocks for now
The outlet warns the rebound may not last
Investors still face other unresolved concerns

685a662a313a.headline: Marcia Ann Gillespie, Editor Who Led Essence and Ms. Magazines, Dies at 82
body: Marcia Ann Gillespie, who served as editor in chief of both Essence and Ms. magazines, has died at age 82, The New York Times reported on November 23, 2026.

According to the Times, Gillespie became editor in chief of Essence when she was just 26 years old. That is an age at which many people are still figuring out which coffee order suits them, let alone running a national magazine.

She later went on to lead Ms., the feminist magazine. The material available does not provide further details on her tenure, the cause of death, or the date and place of her passing, so we will not guess at them.

Even from these sparse facts, the arc of her career says something about the media business. Editors who head magazines with distinct, loyal audiences shape what readers talk about, and Essence and Ms. each built their identities around perspectives that mainstream publications often overlooked.

For readers of the business pages, the story is also a reminder of how much influence a single editor can have over a publication's voice, its audience and, ultimately, its commercial value. Magazines live and die by that editorial identity.
685a662a313a.summary: Marcia Ann Gillespie, who became editor in chief of Essence at 26 and later led the feminist magazine Ms., has died at 82, according to The New York Times.
685a662a313a.why_it_matters: Editors like Gillespie shape the voice and identity that give niche magazines their audience and commercial value. Her career is a case study in how media brands are built around distinct editorial leadership.
key_points: Marcia Ann Gillespie has died at age 82, per The New York Times.
She became editor in chief of Essence at age 26.
She later led the feminist magazine Ms.

29fd82f261e4.headline: Apple Watch SE 3 hits record-low $179 on Amazon for Black Friday, a $70 cut
body: Amazon has dropped the price of the Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS, 40mm) to $179, down from its $249 list price, according to Digital Trends. That $70 discount marks the lowest price the watch has seen since it launched, just in time for Black Friday shopping.

The SE line has long been Apple's budget-friendly pick, and this deal sharpens that pitch. The watch mirrors iPhone notifications, lets you reply to iMessages, WhatsApp texts and other alerts by keyboard or voice, and handles calls and media playback in the usual way.

On health, Apple has widened the toolkit. The SE 3 offers the Vitals app for deeper insights, cycle tracking with temperature sensing, sleep apnea notifications, sleep score tracking and continuous heart rate monitoring.

Safety features are also on board: Fall Detection, Crash Detection, Emergency SOS and Check In. Digital Trends suggests that makes it a reasonable gift for parents or older relatives. The watch also supports Siri AI for pulling up information from your wrist.

There are trade-offs. The SE 3 lacks ECG, blood oxygen tracking and hypertension notifications. Shoppers who want those features would need to step up to the pricier Apple Watch Series 12, so the saving comes with a clear feature ceiling.
29fd82f261e4.summary: Amazon is selling the Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS, 40mm) for $179, $70 under its $249 list price and its lowest since launch, though it skips ECG and blood oxygen tracking.
29fd82f261e4.pixel_take: Seventy dollars off a smartwatch: finally, a way to be nagged about standing up more for less money.
29fd82f261e4.why_it_matters: Record-low pricing on a mainstream wearable shows how retailers use Black Friday to pull shoppers into an ecosystem. For buyers, a cheaper entry point can mean real savings, as long as the missing health sensors don't matter to you.
key_points: Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS, 40mm) is $179 on Amazon, down from $249.
It's the lowest price since the watch launched, per Digital Trends.
It lacks ECG, blood oxygen tracking and hypertension notifications found on the Series 12.

847d428a23da.headline: Is a tiny 'asteroid' really a lost Soviet probe? Scientists argue over 1998 KY26's odd speed-up
body: A small object called 1998 KY26, long classed as an asteroid, is picking up speed in a way gravity alone can't explain, according to Metro's report on a Georgia Institute of Technology study. It is about 36 feet long, spins once every 5.35 minutes and sits roughly 189 million away from Earth, per the article.

The European Space Agency says it will pass within 32 million miles of us in 2028, then come closer still, within 10 million miles, in 2039. The odd acceleration was spotted in 2023, after about 25 years of telescope observations.

Aerospace engineers Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi concluded the speed-up isn't down to a natural phenomenon, writing that it is likely a dehydrated asteroid. That matters because one rival idea, the 'dark comet' theory, holds that hidden ice turning to gas gives such objects a gentle push. But no tail or dust cloud has been seen, and the object is reportedly too warm to carry ice.

Enter Harvard professor Avi Loeb, with co-authors Adam Hibberd and Adam Crowl. They argue the size, shape and strange motion fit a manmade object, specifically Phobos 1, a Soviet craft launched in 1988 that vanished months into its trip to Mars. Their proposal is that sunlight pushing on shiny metal surfaces and solar panels, called solar radiation pressure, is nudging it along. Loeb said the similar orbits suggest the two are the same object.

The debate should get a real test. A Japanese probe, Hayabusa 2, is set to reach the object in 2031 and would be the first spacecraft to study something that small. Loeb predicts its cameras will show a 'Made in the U.S.S.R.' label rather than an iceberg.
847d428a23da.summary: A tiny object called 1998 KY26 is speeding up unexpectedly. Harvard's Avi Loeb says it may be the lost Soviet Phobos 1 probe, while others disagree. Japan's Hayabusa 2 should settle it in 2031.
847d428a23da.pixel_take: If Hayabusa 2 finds a Soviet sticker, it's the longest-overdue delivery in history. If it finds rock, Loeb will still be the only one who got a headline out of it.
847d428a23da.why_it_matters: Small-body science feeds into planetary defense and the growing business of space missions, where knowing what an object is made of matters. A confirmed case of sunlight pushing a lost probe or an odd asteroid would also sharpen how agencies predict orbits.
key_points: 1998 KY26 is accelerating in a way gravity doesn't explain, and no tail or dust has been seen.
Avi Loeb suggests it is the lost Soviet Phobos 1 probe; the Georgia Tech study calls it a likely dehydrated asteroid.
Japan's Hayabusa 2 is due to reach it in 2031.

3bb3b65d8d33.headline: Gaza's Hearing Aid Battery Shortage Leaves Thousands Struggling to Hear
body: Israeli restrictions on goods entering Gaza have left the territory with a severe shortage of hearing aid batteries, according to Al Jazeera. The shortage is cutting thousands of people off from the ability to hear and communicate.

The report says the war has made the problem worse. Thousands of people have developed hearing loss after exposure to explosions and other loud noises, which means demand for hearing devices and the power sources that run them is rising just as supply is choked off.

Hearing aids are small, but they depend on a steady flow of replacement batteries, which typically need changing often. Without them, even a device that works perfectly becomes useless. For users, that can mean being unable to follow conversations, hear warnings or interact with family and aid workers.

The material provided does not give figures on how many batteries are missing, or details of which specific rules are blocking them. It also does not include responses from Israeli officials. Those gaps matter, and further reporting would be needed to understand how the restrictions are applied.

The story is a reminder that humanitarian crises are not only about food, water and shelter. Basic medical and assistive supplies, often low-cost and easy to overlook, can be among the first things to run short when access to goods is limited.
3bb3b65d8d33.summary: Israeli restrictions have caused a severe shortage of hearing aid batteries in Gaza, according to Al Jazeera, leaving thousands unable to hear properly while war-related hearing loss keeps growing.
3bb3b65d8d33.why_it_matters: Restrictions on small, cheap goods can have outsized human costs, and they show how supply controls ripple through health systems. For markets and policymakers, access to basic medical supplies is a key measure of how any aid and reconstruction effort is working.
key_points: Israeli restrictions have caused a severe shortage of hearing aid batteries in Gaza, per Al Jazeera.
Thousands of people are cut off from hearing and communication.
War has added to demand, with thousands developing hearing loss from explosions and loud noise.

772e8ef098cb.headline: 'MoldyRoost' Ad Campaign Can Lift Crypto Recovery Phrases From iPhones With One Tap
body: A malicious advertising campaign dubbed 'MoldyRoost' can steal crypto wallet recovery phrases from iPhones, according to a Cointelegraph report published on November 23, 2026. The operation reportedly used at least 480 ad domains to reach users in more than 47 countries.

The most unsettling detail is how little the victim has to do. According to the report, a single tap could be enough to infect a vulnerable iPhone. The word 'vulnerable' matters here: the attack appears to depend on devices that are not fully protected, though the material available does not spell out the technical details.

The target is the recovery phrase, the string of words that works as the master key to a crypto wallet. Whoever holds it can typically move the funds, and unlike a bank transfer, a blockchain transaction usually cannot be reversed. That makes these phrases a favorite prize for criminals.

The campaign also shows why online ads remain a handy delivery route for attackers. Ads appear on legitimate sites, reach huge audiences and can be spread across many domains, which makes them harder to block one by one. Hundreds of domains across dozens of countries suggests an operation built for scale, not a one-off trick.

The report's source material does not say how many people were affected or how much was stolen, so those questions remain open. For now, the practical lessons are familiar ones: keep devices updated, be wary of tapping ads, and never type a recovery phrase into a website or app prompt you did not seek out yourself.
772e8ef098cb.summary: Cointelegraph reports a campaign called 'MoldyRoost' used at least 480 ad domains in over 47 countries to steal crypto recovery phrases, infecting vulnerable iPhones with a single tap.
772e8ef098cb.pixel_take: A recovery phrase is the one secret you never share, and apparently one stray thumb tap on an ad is all it takes to hand it over. Your phone's 'ignore' button just got promoted.
772e8ef098cb.why_it_matters: Crypto holders carry their own security, and a stolen recovery phrase usually means irreversible losses with no bank to call. Malicious ads show that risk can arrive through ordinary browsing. Keeping devices updated is now basic financial hygiene.
key_points: 'MoldyRoost' used at least 480 ad domains targeting users in more than 47 countries.
A single tap could infect a vulnerable iPhone, per the report.
The goal is stealing crypto wallet recovery phrases, which can unlock funds.

f2286b4f32ed.headline: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Reversing Its Own Removal Decision
body: Nvidia has brought Jensen Huang back as chief executive, according to The Guardian, reversing a decision the chipmaker had made to remove him. The report, published on 23 November 2026, describes the move as stunning.

The Guardian's teaser says the original removal followed reports of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The full text of the article was not available to us, so details of the allegations, the board's reasoning and the timeline of the reversal are not covered here.

What we can say is that a company swapping its chief executive out and then back in is a rare spectacle. Boardrooms usually like their dramatic U-turns to take longer than a news cycle, and Nvidia has apparently compressed the whole saga into something resembling a streaming series.

The context matters. Nvidia is one of the most closely watched companies in technology, a leading maker of chips used in artificial intelligence. Leadership questions at a firm of that profile tend to draw attention from investors, customers and governments alike, especially when a link to China, however alleged, enters the conversation.

Questions remain about how the decision was made, who pushed for the reversal and what safeguards or reviews, if any, are now in place. Until Nvidia or other outlets fill in those gaps, the story rests on The Guardian's reporting and its brief description of events.
f2286b4f32ed.summary: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, reversing its decision to remove him after reports of affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, according to The Guardian.
f2286b4f32ed.pixel_take: A CEO fired and rehired in record time. Even the chips Nvidia makes need longer to process a decision like that.
f2286b4f32ed.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the heart of the AI boom, so who runs it matters to investors, partners and anyone with tech stocks in their portfolio. Leadership turmoil, plus an alleged China link, raises governance and national-security questions that can move markets.
key_points: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, per The Guardian.
The company had earlier decided to remove him after reports of affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Full details of the reversal were not available in the source material.
